title: State of Washington v. Bowman
questions: Does the compulsory collection of DNA samples from persons convicted of felonies constitute an unreasonable search barred by the Fourth Amendment?

title: Arturo Alejandre and Norma Alejandre, husband and wife, Respondents, v. Mary M. Bull, a single person, Petitioner
facts: Respondent Arturo Alejandre and his wife Norma purchased a home from respondent Mary Bull. After the Alejandres subsequently discovered that the home’s septic system was defective, they filed suit against Bull in the Superior Court for Walla Walla County, claiming fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation. The trial court granted summary judgment for Bull, ruling that the Alejandres’ claims are barred by the economic loss rule, which bars recovery for breaches of tort duties where a contractual relationship exists between the parties and the losses are economic losses. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case for trial, holding that the economic loss rule is inapplicable insofar as the contract between Bull and the Alejandres did not allocate risk for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation. Bull appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the Alejandres’ claims barred by the economic loss rule despite the fact that their contract with Bull did not allocate risk for fraudulent or negligent misrepresentation?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Alejandres’ negligent misrepresentation claim is barred by the economic loss rule insofar as the economic loss rule applies regardless of whether the specific risk of loss at issue was allocated in the parties’ contract. The Court also held that although the Alejandres’ claim of fraudulent misrepresentation is not barred by the economic loss rule, the Alejandres failed to present sufficient evidence of fraud given that they failed to exercise the diligence required in investigating the condition of the septic system.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Smith
facts: Petitioner Sarah Smith was convicted of second degree assault with a deadly weapon in the Superior Court for Pierce County after a trial in which the jury was instructed that a person commits second degree assault when under circumstances not amounting to first degree assault they assault another with a deadly weapon. The jury was also given additional instructions setting forth the three common law definitions of assault. Smith appealed her conviction, asserting that these definitions constituted alternative means of committing the crime and that her right to a unanimous jury verdict was violated when the state of Washington failed to present substantial evidence to support convicting her under each of these definitions. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Smith’s conviction. Smith appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the common law definitions of assault that were provided to the jury constitute alternative means of committing the crime?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the common law definitions of assault that were provided to the jury were not alternative means of committing the crime as these definitions merely define the element of assault.

title: Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant County, Washington, a municipal corporation, Respondent, v. North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries , a Washington limited liability company, PACIFIC Northwest Bank, a Washington banking corporation, Petitioners
facts: After failing to reach an agreement with petitioner North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries, L.L.C. to purchase land that it was leasing, the respondent Public Utility District #2 of Grant County decided to acquire the property by condemnation. The Public Utility District subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for Grant County to condemn the property. The superior court condemned the property, ruling that the Public Utility District had complied with the statutory notice requirements for the initiation of an eminent domain action and had established public use and necessity. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. North American Foreign Trade Zone Industries appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Public Utility District comply with the statutory notice requirements for the initiation of an eminent domain action? If so, did the Public Utility District establish public use and necessity?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the notice the Public Utility District provided to the public of the meeting of the Grant County Commission authorizing the condemnation of the property satisfied the notice requirements of Washington Revised Code §35.22.288, Washington Revised Code §35.23.221, Washington Revised Code §35.27.300, and Washington Revised Code §35.30.010. The Court also held that the Public Utility district established that the condemnation was for a public use as the purpose of the condemnation was to allow the Public Utility District to continue operating generators on the property in order to continue providing energy to its customers. Furthermore, the Court found that the condemnation was also necessary insofar as the decision to install the generators was motivated by the need for a backup facility in the event of an interruption in the supply of energy from other sources.

title: State of Washington v. Young
questions: Did the trial court improperly admit hearsay statements made by the victim of an alleged molestation when the hearsay statements were the only evidence that the molestation occurred and the victim later recanted her allegation?

title: State of Washington v. Pillatos
facts: Respondent David Pillatos pled guilty to first degree murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Prior to sentencing, the United States Supreme Court decided in Blakely v. Washington that aggravating factors supporting an exceptional sentence must be proven to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the state of Washington moved to empanel a sentencing jury. The trial court denied the motion, ruling that the procedures set forth in the new provisions of Washington Revised Code §9.94A, which was amended in response to Blakely, cannot be applied retroactively and that it lacks the inherent authority to empanel a sentencing jury. The state of Washington appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do trial courts have the inherent authority to empanel sentencing juries?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that trial courts do not have the inherent authority to bring the unamended version of §9.94A’s procedures into conformity with Blakely as to permit them to do so would usurp powers reserved for the legislature.

title: Chuong Van Pham, an individual, and Heliodoro Lara, an individual, Respondents, v. The City of Seattle, Seattle City Light, Petitioner
questions: City of Seattle discriminated against Pham and Lara. Are they entitled to a supplemental judgment to offset the federal income tax consequences of emotional distress damages awarded by the jury?
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Tami Davis, as personal representative of the Estate of Alan Davis, deceased; and as trustee for Tami Davis and Melissa Davis for the wrongful death of their father, Alan Davis, Appellant, v. Baugh Industrial Contractors , a Washington corporation; E.J. Rody & Sons , a Washington corporation; Gray & Osborne, Inc.; Selpeco Resources , and Selpeco Resources A Knight Piesold Company, Washington corporations; Tucci & Sons , a Washington corporation; Taiheiyo Cement Corporation and Taiheiyo Cement U.S.A. , foreign corporations; Weyerhaeuser Company, and Weyerhaeuser Real Estate Company, Washington corporations; and “Unknown Business Entities I-X,” jointly and severally, Respondents
questions: Under the common-law rule of completion and acceptance a contractor’s liability for negligent acts is extinguished when construction work has been completed and accepted by the owner. The Court must decide whether to recognize a new exception to the rule.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Silverstreak, Inc. v. Department of Labor and Industries
facts: Respondent fill material suppliers Silverstreak et al. sought judicial review of petitioner Washington Department of Labor and Industries (Department) decision that their end-up truck drivers were entitled to prevailing wages under Wash. Rev. Code §39.12.020. The Superior Court for King County entered a judgment upholding the administrative action, and Silverstreak et al subsequently appealed. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court, granted judgment in favor of Silverstreak et al, and remanded the case for further proceedings, holding that the drivers did not qualify to be paid the statutory prevailing wages because their activities at the work site did not involve incorporating the delivered material into the Sea-Tac Third Runway Embankment Project in a fashion similar to spreading, leveling, or rolling. The Supreme Court of Washington granted the Department’s petition for review.
questions: Is the group of workers who drove the end-dump trucks for the fill material suppliers on the first phase of the construction project entitled to be paid prevailing wages under Wash. Rev. Code §39.12.020?
conclusions: Chief Justice Gerry Alexander’s opinion for the Court held that the Court of Appeals erred in applying the canon of ejusdem generis to limit the scope of Prevailing Wage Act’s coverage to only those activities similar to spreading, leveling, or rolling. Consequently, the Court upheld the Department’s broader construction of Wash. Rev. Code §38.12.020, concluding that the end-dump truck drivers did participate in the incorporation of fill material into the Sea-Tac Third Runway Embankment Project. However, the Court estopped the Department’s enforcement of its order because the Department’s position on the applicability of the Prevailing Wage Act in this case is inconsistent with the position in its 1992 policy memorandum and with subsequent representation it made to Silverstreak Inc and the other fill material suppliers. Thus, though on different grounds, the Court affirmed the Court of Appeals determination that the end-dump truck drivers employed by the fill material suppliers were not entitled to prevailing wages.

title: State of Washington v. Athan
facts: Petitioner John Athan was convicted of second degree murder in the Superior Court for King County after a trial in which D.N.A. evidence linking Athan to the victim was admitted. The state of Washington had been able to obtain a sample of Athan’s D.N.A., match it to D.N.A. recovered from the victim, and charge Athan with the murder after detectives from the Seattle Police Department posing as a fictitious law firm sent Athan a letter inviting him to join a fictitious class action lawsuit. When Athan returned the enclosed authorization, the Seattle Police Department was able to recover D.N.A. from his saliva. Athan appealed his conviction directly to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the manner in which his D.N.A. was obtained violated his right to privacy under Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution and the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s prohibition against unreasonable searches and seizures. Athan also asserted that the case should have been dismissed pursuant to Washington Court Rule 8.3(b) on grounds of governmental misconduct.
questions: Did the manner in which Athan’s D.N.A. was obtained violate his right to privacy under Article I §7? Did the manner in which Athan’s D.N.A. was obtained violate the 4th Amendment’s prohibition against unreasonable searches and seizures? Did the Seattle Police Department’s impersonation of a law firm constitute governmental misconduct warranting dismissal pursuant to Washington Court Rule 8.3(b)?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed Athan’s conviction, concluding that no privacy interest exists in voluntarily relinquished saliva and that although the Seattle Police Department violated laws against the unauthorized practice of law in obtaining Athan’s D.N.A., public policy allows a limited amount of deceitful police conduct to detect and eliminate criminal activity. Thus, as the Seattle Police Department’s actions were not so shocking that they violated fundamental fairness, dismissal pursuant to Washington Court Rule 8.3(b) would have been inappropriate.

title: State of Washington v. Jorden
facts: Petitioner Timothy Jorden was convicted of possession of cocaine in the Superior Court for Pierce County after police officers conducted a random check of the registry of the hotel at which he was staying, discovered that there was an outstanding warrant for his arrest, and entered his room, where they found cocaine. Jorden appealed his conviction, asserting that the random check of the hotel registry violated his right to privacy under Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Jorden’s conviction. Jorden appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the information contained in a hotel registry constitute a private affair under Article I §7?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the random check of the hotel registry violated Jorden’s right to privacy insofar as the information contained in the registry reveals sensitive, discreet, and private information about the hotel’s guests.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Kirkman
facts: Respondent Charles Kirkman was convicted of first degree rape in the Superior Court for Clark County after a police officer and medical expert had testified during his trial that the alleged victim's statements to police were clear and consistent. Kirkman appealed his conviction to the Washington Court of Appeals, which reversed the conviction on grounds that these statements were conclusory and violated the exclusive right of the jury to determine guilt. The state of Washington appealed the Washington Court of Appeals' decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the opinions offered to support the alleged victim's credibility invade the jury's exclusive right under the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution to make determinations regarding guilt?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson's opinion for the Court held that neither statement commenting upon the alleged victim's clarity and consistency constituted an improper opinion implying guilt since neither directly commented upon the alleged victim's credibility as a witness may give a statement that is clear and consistent yet nonetheless false. Thus, the Court concluded that the jury's exclusive right to determine the facts of the case had not been infringed upon.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Swinomish Indian Tribal Community v. Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board
facts: The petitioner Swinomish Indian Tribal Community challenged Skagit County’s critical areas ordinance, asserting that its “no harm” standard for protecting anadromous fish habitat in agricultural areas does not comply with the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A). The respondent Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board ruled that the ordinance, with the exception of its monitoring program, is in compliance. The Swinomish Indian Tribal Community petitioned the Superior Court for Thurston County to review the decision. While the appeal was pending, Skagit County amended the ordinance. However, the board ruled that the amendments failed to bring the county into full compliance. Skagit County appealed this ruling to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board err in ruling that Skagit County’s “no harm” standard for protecting anadromous fish habitat in agricultural areas complies with the Growth Management Act? Did the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board err in ruling that Skagit County’s monitoring program does not comply with the Growth Management Act?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board, concluding that the Growth Management Act does not require that local governments enhance critical areas, only that they prevent new harm to critical areas. Thus, the Court held that Skagit County’s “no harm” standard complies with the Growth Management Act. The Court also found that the Western Washington Growth Management Hearings Board properly ruled that Skagit County’s amended critical areas ordinance’s monitoring program does not comply with the Growth Management Act.

title: Scott v. Cingular Wireless
facts: Alleging that respondent Cingular Wireless overcharged its customers by unlawfully adding hidden charges, a group of customers led by petitioner Doug Scott initiated a class action against Cingular Wireless. The trial court granted Cingular Wireless’s motion to compel arbitration pursuant to a clause in its standard subscriber contract. Scott appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the enforceability of the clause in Scott’s subscriber contract compelling arbitration and waiving the right to pursue class action litigation governed by the Federal Arbitration Act (9 U.S.C. §§1-16)? If not, is the clause unconscionable and unenforceable under Washington law?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the trial court, concluding that the Federal Arbitration Act does not govern the enforceability of the clause. The Court also held that the clause is unconscionable and unenforceable under Washington law insofar as a class action is often the only effective method of vindicating the public’s rights under the Consumer Protection Act (Washington Revised Code §19.86) when a consumer claim is small but numerous. The Court also found that the clause is unconscionable and unenforceable insofar as it exculpates Cingular Wireless from liability for a large class of wrongful conduct.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Dix v. I.C.T. Group, Inc.
facts: Respondent Suzy Dix and other subscribers to America Online’s internet service filed a class action in the state of Washington against I.C.T. Group, Inc., asserting that I.C.T. Group, which is responsible for handling customer service inquiries for America Online, engaged in deceptive practices in violation of Washington’s Consumer Protection Act (Washington Revised Code §19.86). The trial court dismissed the class action on grounds that the forum selection clause in America Online’s service agreement requires that any claims arising from customers’ use of the service be brought in Virginia. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the forum selection clause is unenforceable insofar as the selected forum of Virginia does not permit class actions, rendering the forum selection clause contrary to the public policy underlying the Consumer Protection Act. I.C.T. Group appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are forum selection clauses requiring that litigation be brought in states that do not permit class actions contrary to the public policy underlying the Consumer Protection Act and therefore unenforceable?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case for trial, concluding that the forum selection clause is contrary to the public policy underlying the Consumer Protection Act. In particular, the Court held that class actions are an important tool for carrying out the Consumer Protection Act’s enforcement scheme given that it would otherwise be economically unfeasible for claims of small value such as Dix’s to be brought.

title: State of Washington v. O'Neal
facts: Petitioner Harry O’Neal was convicted of the manufacture of methamphetamine while armed with a firearm in the Superior Court for Thurston County after a search of his home revealed drug paraphernalia and several firearms. O’Neal appealed the sentencing enhancement arising from the jury’s finding that he committed the crime while armed with a firearm, asserting that the firearms were not easily accessible and readily available and that there was no nexus between him, the manufacture of methamphetamine, and the firearms. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed O’Neal’s conviction. O’Neal appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was O’Neal armed for purposes of sentencing enhancement when he committed the crime of manufacturing methamphetamine?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that there was sufficient evidence for the jury to conclude that there was a nexus between O’Neal, the manufacture of methamphetamine, and the firearms.

title: Biggers v. Bainbridge Island
facts: Respondent Ray Biggers petitioned for a declaratory judgment that Ordinance 2001-45, which was enacted by the petitioner city of Bainbridge Island’s city council and which placed a moratorium upon the filing of new applications for shoreline substantial development permits, exemptions, and conditional use permits, is unconstitutional insofar as it conflicts with the Shoreline Management Act (Washington Revised Code §90.58). The trial court granted summary judgment for Biggers. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. The city of Bainbridge Island appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Ordinance 2001-45 conflict with the Shoreline Management Act?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Ordinance 2001-45 is unconstitutional insofar as Article XVII §1 of the Washington State Constitution vests the power to regulate shorelines in the state of Washington and Ordinance 2001-45 conflicts with the Shoreline Management Act’s exercise of this regulatory power as it prohibits development that would otherwise be permitted under the Shoreline Management Act.

title: Lindeman v. Kelso School District #458
facts: Petitioner Richard Lindeman’s son was involved in an altercation on a school bus that was recorded by a surveillance camera. After the respondent Kelso School District #458 permitted Lindeman to view the videotape of the altercation, Lindeman submitted a request for a copy of the videotape. The Kelso School District denied the request on grounds that the videotape is exempt from release under the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56) insofar as it falls within former Washington Revised Code §42.17.310(1)(a)’s exception for personal information in files maintained for students. Lindeman subsequently filed suit against the Kelso School District in the Superior Court for Cowlitz County, which ruled that the videotape is exempt from disclosure under §42.17.310(1)(a). Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Lindeman appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a videotape of an altercation between two students on a school bus fall within the exception to the Public Records Act’s mandate of disclosure of public records created by §42.17.310(1)(a) for personal information in files maintained for students?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the videotape is not exempt from disclosure under §42.17.310(1)(a). In particular, the Court found that even if the videotape were used as a basis for disciplining a student, the videotape itself is not a student record insofar as it does not reveal whether or what type of discipline was imposed.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Valley, L.L.C. v. Stewart
facts: The law firm Morse & Bratt performed legal work for Neil Rose. When Morse & Bratt expressed concern to Rose regarding his ability to pay his outstanding legal fees, Rose executed a deed of trust to a property owned by petitioner Valley, L.L.C., of which Rose was a member, as security. When Rose subsequently defaulted on his legal fees, respondent Randall Stewart, Morse & Bratt’s trustee, initiated foreclosure proceedings. Valley moved to prevent foreclosure, asserting that Rose lacked authority to pledge Valley’s property as collateral and that the agreement between Rose and Morse & Bratt violated Washington’s Rules of Professional Conduct. The trial court granted summary judgment for Stewart, ruling that Rose had authority to pledge Valley’s property as collateral and that the agreement is enforceable. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Valley appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in granting summary judgment for Stewart?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case to the trial court, concluding that granting summary judgment was inappropriate insofar as material issues of fact exist regarding whether the agreement complied with Washington Rule of Professional Conduct 1.8, which restricts business transactions between attorneys and their clients, and whether Rose had authority to pledge Valley’s property as collateral.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Pasco v. Shaw
facts: Petitioner Bernard Shaw petitioned the Superior Court for Franklin County for a declaratory judgment that Ordinance 3231, which was enacted by the respondent city of Pasco and requires landlords to submit a certification every two years that their rental units meet all applicable health, safety, and building code requirements, violates the right against unreasonable searches conferred by the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution. The superior court granted summary judgment for the city of Pasco, ruling that landlords and the private inspectors that they employ are not state actors and that limited inspections of rental units for purposes of ensuring compliance with health, safety, and building codes are not searches. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed. Shaw appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Ordinance 3231’s requirement that landlords inspect rental units with or without tenant consent subject tenants to unreasonable searches?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that entry into a rental unit for purposes of obtaining a certificate of compliance with health, safety, and building codes is a private action that is intended to benefit the landlord. Thus, as no state action is involved, the 4th Amendment and Article I §7 are not implicated.

title: Bank of America v. Wells Fargo Bank
facts: Sakae and Yuko Sugihara received a home loan from Washington Mutual secured with a deed of trust on the property. The Sugiharas subsequently also took out a business loan with respondent Bank of America that was secured in part with the deed of trust on their home and a home equity loan with petitioner Wells Fargo Bank that paid off the Washington Mutual home loan. After the Sugiharas defaulted on the Bank of America business loan, Bank of America filed suit against the Sugiharas, seeking foreclosure to remedy the default. The superior court ruled that, under the doctrine of equitable subrogation, Wells Fargo Bank succeeded to the rights of Washington Mutual and therefore succeeded to its first priority lien. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the superior court’s ruling, holding that the application of equitable subrogation is barred by the fact that Wells Fargo Bank’s had actual knowledge of Bank of America’s lien on the home at the time that it approved the home equity loan. Wells Fargo Bank appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the fact that Wells Fargo Bank’s had actual knowledge of Bank of America’s lien on the home at the time that it approved the home equity loan bar equitable subrogation?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that there is no need to consider the subrogee’s knowledge of intervening interests and that equitable subrogation should be applied whenever justice requires it and there is no prejudice to junior interests as to hold otherwise would discourage the refinancing of home mortgages and increase the number of foreclosures.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Bostain v. Food Express, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Larie E. Bostain was an interstate truck driver employed by respondent Food Express Inc. out of the company's Vancouver terminal. Bostain was hired under the agreement he would not be paid overtime if he worked over 40 hours, but rather by the mile once over 200 miles. After being terminated for violating federal driving limitations, Bostain filed suit against Food Express for unpaid wages, unpaid overtime, and willful failure to pay wages. The Superior Court for Clark County ruled in favor of Bostain entitling him to overtime payment under Washington’s Minimum Wage Act, Wash. Rev. Code §49.46.130(1), even if driving time occurred outside the employed state of Washington. Food Express appealed, arguing the suit was retaliatory for the termination, and Bostain cross-appealed for higher awards for attorney fees. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court, claiming Bostain was not entitled to overtime payment for work outside the state of Washington. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Bostain’s petition for discretionary review.
questions: Is Wash. Rev. Code §49.46.130(1) applicable to overtime hours worked by Washington-based truck drivers engaged in interstate transportation, regardless of the amount of hours actually worked within Washington state?
conclusions: Justice Barbara A. Madsen's opinion for the Court concluded that Food Express cited no supporting evidence Bostain’s suit was retaliatory, and that the overtime provisions of Wash. Rev. Code §49.46.130(1) do apply to all hours worked by Washington-based truck drivers involved in interstate transportation. Thus, the Court of Appeals ruling was reversed, and the case was remanded to the trial court to recalculate the amount of Bostain’s awarded attorney fees and to determine the attorney fees for the appeal and discretionary review.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Moore
facts: Petitioner Alex Moore was convicted of possession of cocaine with intent to deliver after a search of his person following his arrest for refusing to cooperate with a police officer revealed cocaine and $800 in cash. Moore appealed his conviction, asserting that his arrest and the subsequent search of his person were unlawful insofar as refusing to cooperate with a police officer by providing a false name is not a crime unless the person doing so is being stopped and cited for a traffic violation. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Moore’s conviction, holding that although Moore was not being cited for a traffic violation, he could have been given that his seatbelt was unfastened at the time that the automobile that he was a passenger in was stopped. Moore appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Moore’s arrest for refusing to cooperate with a police officer and the subsequent search of his person unlawful?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the police officer that stopped the automobile that Moore was a passenger in was not investigating the seatbelt infraction when he asked Moore his name, the fact that he could have cited Moore for not having his seatbelt fastened was irrelevant and there was no basis for arresting Moore for refusing to cooperate with a police officer. Thus, the Court ordered the evidence derived from the subsequent search suppressed and remanded the case.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Morin v. Burris
facts: In a consolidation of 3 cases, petitioners Morin, Gutz, and Matia Investment Funds Inc. properly initiated lawsuits against respondents Burris, Johnson, and the City of Tacoma respectively. In all three cases the respondents failed to file answers or formally appear in court when actions where brought against them, resulting in the successful motion for default judgment by the petitioners. The respondents moved to vacate the default judgment, claiming they had informally appeared and were entitled to notice of default proceedings. In the Morin and Matia Investment Funds cases the default judgments were vacated in their respective Superior Courts, while in the Gutz case the motion to vacate was denied. Upon appeal the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court rulings in Morin and Matia Investment Funds. In the Gutz case, the Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the trial court holding the respondent appeared through the insurer, entitling him to notice before entry of the order of default and that the trial court abused its discretion by refusing to vacate the default judgment. The cases were consolidated for review by the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does merely showing informal intent to defend before a case is filed, through prelitigation communication, satisfy the substantial compliance and appearance requirement in the formal litigation process?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court held that informal appearance, according to the substantial compliance doctrine for formal litigation procedures long held by the Court, a mere intent to defend, whether before or after a case is filed, is not enough because acknowledgment that a dispute exist must be made in court. Since the respondents in the Morin and Matia Investment Funds cases did not acknowledge the dispute in court, they were not entitled to notice of the default judgment hearing. Thus, the Court reversed the Court of Appeals and remanded to the trial courts for reentry of default judgments. In the Gutz case, the record showed the petitioners counsel actively concealed the fact that summons and complaint had been filed against the respondent. The trial court appeared to have missed this issue, so the case was remanded for further consideration.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Okeson v. Seattle
facts: In a class action suit against respondent City of Seattle and its municipal utility Seattle City Lights, petitioner and ratepayer Rud Okeson challenged the City utility program to offset and mitigate the effects of its greenhouse gas emissions by paying other public and private entities to reduce theirs. Both parties moved for summary judgment on the legality of the offset program in the Superior Court of King County, where in which summary judgment was granted in favor of the City of Seattle. Okeson appealed contending that paying to reduce emissions from other entities facilities serves a general government purpose and thus making the general taxpayer bear the burden of mitigation expenses, not the utility ratepayers. The Supreme Court of Washington granted review.
questions: Can a municipal utility mitigate the effects of its greenhouse gas emissions by paying other public and private entities to reduce those entities’ emissions? If so, does the utility ratepayer bear the burden of the mitigation expenses or the general taxpayer?
conclusions: Chief Justice Gerry L. Alexander wrote the opinion for the Court holding that according to the implied proprietary functions and actions of a city utility in Wash. Rev. Code §35.92.050, Seattle City Light’s greenhouse gas emission offset contracts are not proprietary because they are not part of the direct electrical services for which the individual utility customary is billed. Furthermore, improving the global environment is a general government purpose and the mitigation expenses derived from the program must be borne by the general taxpayers rather than strictly the utility ratepayers. The Court reversed the trial court’s order granting summary judgment to the City of Seattle, and remanded the case for entry of judgment consistent with this opinion.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Little v. King
facts: Respondent insured driver Lisa Little filed action for damages after sustaining personal injuries from a motor vehicle accident caused by petitioner uninsured negligent driver Annie King. The accident occurred while Little was driving on work-related business, so Little’s counsel notified the employer’s insurer St. Paul Insurance Company of potential liability expenses because of the employer’s uninsured motorist coverage. St. Paul took no action to intervene as an interested party at risk of liability. Little moved for default against King in the Superior Court for King County, in which King declined to file an answer to contest the judgment. The Superior Court entered a default judgment in favor of Little, holding St. Paul liable under the employer’s uninsured motorist coverage obligations. St. Paul moved to intervene, and joined King in a motion to vacate the default judgment arguing the damages awarded were unreasonable and that Little’s preexisting conditions may have contributed to the post-accident injuries. A different Superior Court judge vacated the default judgment, and Little appealed. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s ruling, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted review.
questions: Does King and St. Paul present substantial evidence of a prima facie defense to the damages in the default judgment? Did the trial court abuse its discretion in vacating the default judgment?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court held that first, St. Paul and King did not provide substantial evidence Little’s preexisting conditions “probably” or “more likely than not” caused her post-accident condition, instead merely argued they “might have.” Second, St. Paul’s failure to take the initial opportunity to intervene, along with King’s failure to file an answer to contest the default judgment, do not meet the standards required for a defense of excusable neglect persuant to the equitable basis for vacating the judgment. Thus, the trial court did abuse its discretion in vacating the default judgment. The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals, and remanded the case to the trial court for reinstatement of the judgment.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Colorado Structures, Inc. v. Insurance Company of the West
facts: Respondent Colorado Structures, Inc. subcontracted with Action Excavating and Paving, Inc. to build the sewer system for a Wal-Mart store being constructed by Colorado Structures. When Action Excavating and Paving failed to timely complete its work, Colorado Structures supplemented its crews to minimize cost and delay. Colorado Structures subsequently filed suit against petitioner Insurance Company of the West, Action Excavating and Paving’s surety, in the Superior Court for Clark County in an effort to recover on the performance bond guaranteeing Action Excavating and Paving’s work. The trial court ruled that Insurance Company of the West is liable on the performance bond despite the fact that Colorado Structures had not formally declared Action Excavating and Paving to be in default. However, the trial court declined to award attorney fees to Colorado Structures. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that Insurance Company of the West is liable on the performance bond and that Colorado Structures is also entitled to attorney fees. Insurance Company of the West appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Were Insurance Company of the West’s obligations as a surety conditioned upon Colorado Structures declaring Action Excavating and Paving to be in default? If not, is Colorado Structures also entitled to attorney fees?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Colorado Structures gave Insurance Company of the West adequate prior notice of Action Excavating and Paving’s failure to perform and that it was not required to formally declare Action Excavating and Paving to be in default. The Court also held that Colorado Structures is entitled to attorney fees under the same principle that awards attorney fees to an insured who is compelled to assume the burden of legal action to obtain the benefit of its insurance contract.

title: Voters Education Committee v. Public Disclosure Commission
facts: During the 2004 campaign, the petitioner Voters Education Committee sponsored television advertisements criticizing Deborah Senn, a candidate for attorney general, without registering as a political committee or disclosing information regarding its contributions and expenditures as required by the Fair Campaign Practices Act (Washington Revised Code §42.17). The respondent Public Disclosure Commission subsequently brought an enforcement action against the Voters Education Committee in the Superior Court for Thurston County. In response, the Voters Education Committee petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a declaratory judgment that its advertisements were protected under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §5 of the Washington State Constitution. The Superior Court for King County denied the petition, ruling that §42.17’s disclosure requirements are constitutional. The Voters Education Committee appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the definition of a “political committee” under §42.17 unconstitutionally vague? Does Article I §5 confer greater protection against disclosure requirements than the 1st Amendment?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that §42.17’s use of the phrase “in support of, or opposition to, any candidate” in its definition of a “political committee” is not unconstitutionally vague as a person of ordinary intelligence would have a reasonable opportunity to understand its meaning. The Court also held that there is no reason to believe that the framers of Article I §5 intended to confer greater protection against disclosure requirements than that conferred by the 1st Amendment.

title: San Juan County v. No New Gas Tax
facts: During a regularly scheduled radio program hosted by Kirby Wilbur and John Carlson, Wilbur and Carlson expressed their support for the passage of Initiative 912, which would have repealed a fuel tax enacted by the legislature, and encouraged listeners to make contributions to No New Gas Tax, a political action committee that had been organized to support Initiative 912. After No New Gas Tax failed to report Wilbur and Carlson’s promotional efforts as an in kind campaign contribution, San Juan County filed a complaint against No New Gas Tax that alleged that No New Gas Tax violated the disclosure provisions of the Fair Campaign Practices Act (Washington Revised Code §42.17). The Superior Court for Thurston County ruled that Wilbur and Carlson’s promotional efforts constituted an in kind campaign contribution under §42.17 and ordered No New Gas Tax to report the value of the air time used by Wilbur and Carlson to promote No New Gas Tax and Initiative 912 as a campaign contribution. As complying with §42.17’s $5,000 limit on campaign contributions within three weeks of an election would therefore require Wilbur and Carlson to refrain from any further on air discussion of No New Gas Tax or Initiative 912, No New Gas Tax filed a counterclaim against San Juan County that asserted that its constitutional rights had been violated and sought injunctive relief and an award of attorney’s fees. The superior court dismissed the counterclaim. No New Gas Tax appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Were Wilbur and Carlson’s on air efforts to promote No New Gas Tax and Initiative 912 a campaign contribution subject to disclosure requirements and contribution limits under §42.17?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the superior court, concluding that Wilbur and Carlson’s promotional efforts fell within §42.17’s media exemption insofar as they aired during the content portion of a regularly scheduled radio program for which the broadcaster does not normally require payment on a radio station not controlled by a candidate or political action committee. Thus, as the superior court’s dismissal of No New Gas Tax’s counterclaim had been based upon an incorrect interpretation of §42.17, the Court remanded the case to the superior court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re Detention of Stout
facts: Following a trial, petitioner Roy Stout was civilly committed as a sexually violent predator pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09. Stout subsequently appealed his commitment, asserting that the trial court erred in ruling that he was collaterally estopped from relitigating the facts underlying his conviction for a sexually motivated burglary, that the trial court denied him his right to confrontation under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §22 of the Washington State Constitution by permitting the victim of the burglary to testify via telephonic deposition, that he received ineffective assistance of counsel, and that the trial court failed to make the required legal finding that he has serious difficulty controlling his behavior. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Stout’s commitment. Stout appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Stout collaterally estopped from relitigating the facts underlying his conviction for a sexually motivated burglary? Did permitting the victim of the burglary to testify via telephonic deposition deny Stout his right to confrontation? Did Stout receive ineffective assistance of counsel? Did the trial court err in failing to make a legal finding that Stout has serious difficulty controlling his behavior?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the fact that Stout pled guilty to the burglary collaterally estops him from relitigating the facts of the case. The Court also held that as civil commitment trials are not criminal proceedings, an accused sexually violent predator does not have a right to confrontation given the various procedural safeguards associated with such trials. The Court also found that the failure of Stout’s attorney to object to the state’s introduction of evidence relating to an incident in which Stout was accused of rape but ultimately acquitted did not constitute ineffective assistance of counsel insofar as Stout failed to show that the state was collaterally estopped by his acquittal from introducing such evidence. Finally, the Court held that the trial court did not err in failing to make a legal finding that Stout has serious difficulty controlling his behavior as this is not an element that the state is required to prove.

title: Sanders v. Seattle
facts: Petitioners Beth Sanders and other Iraq War protesters sought declaratory and injunctive relief on a claim that their constitutionally protected freedom of speech was unlawfully restricted by the City of Seattle. The protesters were repeatedly asked by security personnel of a privately owned shopping mall to hold their stick-mounted signs down while on the property. The protesters claimed the shopping mall was subject to municipal easement for access to a boarding platform for a monorail station attached to the exterior of the mall, and was therefore a public forum. The King County Superior Court entered a summary judgment in favor of the City of Seattle, holding that the easement portion of the mall is properly characterized as a nonpublic forum. The notice of appeal was transferred to the Supreme Court of Washington for direct review.
questions: Is the mall property, subject to the City’s easement, a public forum? Did the security personnel’s conduct infringe on the protesters’ free speech rights under the Washington Constitution? Can the protesters bring facial challenges to the easement contract between the City and the mall owner?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the judgment of the trial court, holding that since the City’s easement is located in the interior of the privately owned shopping mall, the property is not considered to be a public forum. Furthermore, the security personnel’s conduct did not infringe on the protesters’ constitutional free speech rights because the mall owner’s oral policy requiring persons using the interior public easement to hold stick-mounted signs down for public safety is a reasonable regulation on speech. Finally, given that the interior easement is a nonpublic forum, the protesters cannot bring facial challenges to the easement contract.

title: Medina v. Primm
facts: Petitioner Melody Primm was charged by the respondent city of Medina with driving under the influence of alcohol. Pursuant to an agreement between the city of Medina and the city of Kirkland to share municipal court facilities, the case was heard in Kirkland in the courthouse of the Kirkland Municipal Court. Primm moved to dismiss the charge for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, asserting that the Kirkland Municipal Court lacks jurisdiction to adjudicate cases involving alleged violations of the Medina Municipal Code. The municipal court denied the motion. Upon appeal, the Superior Court for King County affirmed, holding that a city’s municipal court may hear cases in a courthouse located outside of city limits. Primm appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a city’s municipal court have jurisdiction to hear cases in the court facilities of a different city?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that although Washington Revised Code §39.34.180 only expressly authorizes interlocal agreements between cities and counties, the authority for cities to contract with one another to provide court services predates §39.34.180 and is reflected in a number of statutes that regulate the terms of such agreements. Thus, as there is no indication that the legislature intended to repeal this authority when it enacted §39.34.180, the Court held that the municipal court had jurisdiction to hear Primm’s case.

title: Ford Motor Company v. Seattle
facts: Petitioner Ford Motor Company petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a declaratory judgment that its liability to the respondent city of Seattle for business and occupation taxes had been improperly calculated. The superior court granted summary judgment for the city of Seattle, ruling that business and occupation taxes had been properly assessed on the entire gross proceeds of vehicles that Ford Motor Company sold at wholesale to its dealers in Seattle. Ford Motor Company appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Ford Motor Company engaged in the business of making wholesale sales in the city of Seattle? If so, was Ford Motor Company’s tax liability properly apportioned? Does the tax unduly burden interstate commerce?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that although the actual sales at wholesale occur in Michigan, Ford Motor Company’s other business activities in Seattle related to its wholesale sales to its dealers nonetheless subject it to business and occupation taxes for the privilege of doing business in the city. The Court also held that Ford Motor Company’s tax liability can be based upon the gross proceeds of its wholesale sales to its dealers in Seattle and need not be limited to the portion of Ford Motor Company’s gross income attributable to its actual business activities in Seattle. Finally, the Court found that the tax does not unduly burden interstate commerce insofar as it is applied to an activity with a substantial nexus with the city of Seattle, is fairly apportioned, and does not discriminate against interstate commerce.

title: Madison v. State of Washington
facts: Respondents Daniel Madison and other convicted felons sought reinstatement of their voting rights through a declaration that the State’s disenfranchisement scheme, Wash. Rev. Code §9.94A.637, is unconstitutional. They argued it denies convicted felons the right to vote if they have not fully paid legal financial obligations included as a part of their sentences. Specifically, the disenfranchisement scheme violates the privileges and immunities clause (Art. I, Sect. 12) of the State Constitution as well as the equal protection clause (Amend. XIV) of the Federal Constitution because it denied them the right to vote based on their financial status. The Superior Court for King County entered a summary judgment in favor of the respondents. The State petitioned for direct review to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the State’s disenfranchisement scheme violate the privileges and immunities clause of the State’s Constitution or the equal protection clause of the United States Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Mary E. Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court held that the Washington State Constitution’s privileges and immunities clause only recognizes the increased protection for those individuals who currently possess the fundamental right to vote, and not to felons whose voting rights have been stripped. Thus, the State’s disenfranchisement scheme does not violate the State Constitutional provision. Furthermore, since the State provision actually guarantees more right to vote protection than the equal protection clause of the Federal Constitution, the disenfranchisement scheme does not violate the federal provision. The Court reversed the Superior Court’s summary judgment.

title: Rickert v. Public Disclosure Commission
facts: During her unsuccessful campaign against Senator Tim Sheldon, respondent Marilou Rickert sponsored a mailing that contained several false statements regarding Sheldon’s record. Sheldon subsequently filed a complaint with the Public Disclosure Commission that asserted that Rickert violated Washington Revised Code §42.17.530(1), which prohibits the sponsorship with actual malice of political advertising or electioneering communication that contains a false statement of material fact about a candidate for public office. Following a hearing, the Public Disclosure Commission fined Rickert $1,000, concluding that the mailing contained false statements that were material and that Rickert sponsored the mailing with actual malice. Rickert appealed the Public Disclosure Commission’s decision on grounds that §42.17.530(1) infringes the right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I §5 of the Washington State Constitution. The Washington Court of Appeals overturned the Public Disclosure Commission’s ruling and sanction, holding that §42.17.530(1) is unconstitutional. The Public Disclosure Commission appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §42.17.530(1) infringe the right to freedom of speech and expression?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that §42.17.530(1) proscribes constitutionally protected speech insofar as it is not limited to defamatory statements and that it does not survive strict scrutiny. In particular, the Court held that not only is protecting candidates for public office not a compelling interest, §42.17.530(1) is not narrowly tailored to further this interest as it does not apply to other types of statements that implicate the state’s interest in protecting the integrity of elections. The Court also found that §42.17.530(1) is constitutionally infirm insofar as it is likely to have a chilling effect upon constitutionally protected speech given that it is enforced by an unelected administrative body with no requirement that a reviewing court conduct a de novo review.

title: State of Washington v. Stockwell
facts: Petitioner Dan Stockwell was tried and convicted in Kitsap County Superior Court of first-degree child molestation and attempted child molestation of two of his wife’s granddaughters. Stockwell was previously convicted of first degree statutory rape in 1986, and given this prior rape conviction the State successfully sought a life sentence under the Persistent Offender Accountability Act (POAA), former Wash. Rev. Code § 9.94A.030(32)(b), recodified as Wash. Rev. Code §9.94A.030(33)(b); §9.94A.570. Stockwell appealed the sentence, arguing that his prior sentence is neither listed nor comparable to a strike offense under the POAA, and thus he was not eligible for life sentence. Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Stockwell’s petition for review.
questions: Is first-degree rape of a child and first degree statutory rape of a child legally comparable crimes pursuant to Wash. Rev. Code §9.94.030; §9.94A.570?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court held that, given legislative intent in Wash. Rev. Code §9.94A.030(33)(b); §9.94A.570 that nonmarriage intercourse with a child 10 years old or less is an implied element of first-degree statutory rape, along with its later addition of the comparability clause , as a matter of law Stockwell’s prior conviction of first degree statutory rape is subject to comparablility analysis. Thus, his prior conviction does qualify as a “strike” under the two strikes provision of the POAA. Finding that the offenses are comparable, the Court affirmed Stockwell’s life sentence.

title: Soltero v. Wimer
facts: Petitioner Kenneth Wimer and respondent Patricia Soltero were engaged in a meretricious relationship, a marital-like relationship where both parties cohabitate with knowledge that a lawful marriage between them does not exist, for nine years. When Wimer terminated the relationship, Soltero brought a lawsuit seeking a distribution of their assets. The trial court found that Wimer and Soltero had a meretricious relationship and that Soltero’s provision of domestic services to Wimer during the relationship entitles her to an equitable share of the parties’ earnings during the relationship and therefore ordered Wimer to pay Soltero $135,000. Wimer appealed the trial court’s decision, asserting that the trial court erred in awarding Soltero $135,000 insofar as the trial court identified no community-like property owned jointly by both parties. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Wimer appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the separate property of parties in a dissolving meretricious relationship subject to equitable distribution?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the trial court erred in awarding Soltero $135,000 from Wimer’s separate assets insofar as the separate property of parties in a dissolving meretricious relationship is not subject to equitable distribution.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Sleasman v. Lacey
facts: Petitioner property owners Stephen Sleasman and wife sought judicial review of a hearing examiner’s upholding of respondent City of Lacey’s decision to impose a monetary sanction for Sleasman's removal of several trees from their property without a permit, violating Lacey, Wash., Code §14.32.030. The Thurston County Superior Court entered a judgment upholding the hearing examiner’s decision, holding the Sleasman’s property was “partially developed” according to the language in Lacey, Wash., Code §14.32.020, which was clear, unambiguous, and not unconstitutionally vague as the Sleasman’s argued. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment and findings, and the Sleasman’s appealed again to the Supreme Court of Washington for review.
questions: Does the Sleasman’s property qualify as “underdeveloped” or “partially developed” according to Lacey, Wash., Code §14.32.020, thus making the removal of trees without a permit susceptible to monetary sanction? Is the tree removal ordinance constitutionally vague?
conclusions: Justice Richard Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court agreed with the Court of Appeals that Lacey, Wash., Code §14.32.020 is clear and unambiguous; however it is inapplicable in this case. The ordinance only applies to “underdeveloped” and “partially developed” property, but under the term's plain meaning the Sleasman’s property is “developed.” Their property qualifies as “developed” because it is a lawful building site that is already suited for sale or use, and it is irrelevant that the Sleasman’s may further improve the property. Concluding that the Court of Appeals misapplied the definitions in the ordinance, the Court reversed its decision and judgment.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Woo v. Fireman's Fund Insurance Company
facts: Tina Alberts filed suit against her oral surgeon, respondent Robert Woo, after Woo inserted imitation boar tusks in Alberts’ mouth and photographed her while she was under anesthesia during a dental procedure. Although Woo maintained a liability insurance policy with respondent Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company, Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company refused to defend Woo on grounds that the conduct that gave rise to Alberts’ lawsuit did not occur in the course of the provision of dental services. After Woo reached a settlement agreement with Alberts, he filed suit against Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company, asserting that it breached its duty to defend him under the policy. The jury returned a verdict for Woo. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company did not have a duty to defend Woo against Alberts’ lawsuit. Woo appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company breach its duty to defend Woo under his liability insurance policy?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated the jury’s verdict, concluding that Fireman’s Fund Insurance Company breached its duty to defend Woo because the conduct that gave rise to Alberts’ lawsuit conceivably fell within Woo’s liability insurance policy’s broad definition of the practice of dentistry.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Brown
facts: Petitioner Mickey Brown was convicted of first degree burglary while armed with a deadly weapon and intimidating a witness after burglarizing a home and warning his roommate not to provide information to the police regarding the burglary. Brown appealed his conviction for intimidating a witness and his deadly weapon enhancement, asserting that the threat he made to his roommate did not constitute an attempt to influence their testimony and that the fact that the victim found that their rifle had been moved from a closet to a bed is insufficient to establish he was armed with a deadly weapon during the burglary. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Brown’s convictions. Brown appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the threat Brown made to his roommate constitute the intimidation of a witness under Washington Revised Code §9A.72.110? Was Brown armed with a deadly weapon during the burglary?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Brown’s threat did not constitute the intimidation of a witness under Washington Revised Code §9A.72.110 insofar as the state did not prove that Brown threatened his roommate in an attempt to influence their testimony, only that Brown threatened his roommate in attempt to prevent them from providing any information to the police regarding the burglary. The Court also held that the fact that the rifle had been moved from a closet to a bed is insufficient to establish that Brown was armed with a deadly weapon during the burglary insofar as no evidence was presented that Brown had handled the weapon in a manner indicative of an intent or willingness to use it in furtherance of the crime.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Marshall
facts: The respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board recommended that petitioner Bradley Marshall be disbarred after finding that Marshall violated several rules of professional conduct in the course of his representation of a group of longshoremen bringing racial discrimination claims against their unions. In particular, the disciplinary board found that Marshall improperly shared his fees with a non-lawyer, subsequently attempted to conceal the fee-sharing arrangement, inflated his costs, failed to provide proper accounting to his clients, failed to properly advise his clients of the risks of multiple representation, and filed an appeal without their authorization. Marshall appealed the disciplinary board’s findings and sanction to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that he had acted negligently rather than knowingly, that he was not given adequate notice of the charges against him or the possible sanctions involved, and that the sanction imposed is disproportionate to the violations committed.
questions: Are the disciplinary board’s findings of fact supported by substantial evidence? If so, is disbarment an appropriate sanction? Was Marshall denied due process?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the disciplinary board, concluding that Marshall had not improperly shared his fees with a non-lawyer insofar as the alleged fee-sharing merely involved Marshall carrying out a preexisting agreement between his clients and a third party for that third party to receive a portion of the clients’ settlement as a consulting fee. However, the Court held that substantial evidence supports the disciplinary board’s other findings of fact. The Court also found that Marshall was not denied due process as he had been fully apprised of the charges against him and the possible sanctions involved. Thus, given that the Court found that no improper fee-sharing had occurred and given the lack of unanimity among the members of the disciplinary board regarding the sanction to be recommended and the sanctions imposed by the Court in similar cases, the Court ordered that Marshall be suspended from the practice of law for eighteen months rather than disbarred.

title: Tingey v. Haisch
facts: Petitioner attorney David L. Tingey sought to recover unpaid attorney fees from respondent client Lloyd Haisch by filing action in Grant County Superior Court, more than three years after the last day Tingey performed legal services for Haisch. Tingey performed legal services for Haisch on an hourly fee basis without a written fee agreement. The trial court entered summary judgment in favor of Tingey, and Haisch subsequently appealed. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s judgment, holding that the transaction between Tingey and Haisch did not involve an open account with ongoing debit and credit entries and a fluctuating left open until either party found it convenient to settle and close. Therefore, the claim for attorney fees was not an account receivable subject to a six-year limitation period as Tingey claimed. Tingey appealed, arguing the Court of Appeals improperly applied the term “account receivable,” and challenged the judgment that his action to collect the fees is not governed by the relevant six-year limitation statute, Wash. Rev. Code §4.16.040(2). The Supreme Court of Washington granted Tingey’s petition for review.
questions: Does the Wash. Rev. Code 4.16.040(2) six-year limitation for an “action upon an account receivable incurred in the ordinary course of business” provide the limitation in an action to collect a balance owed by a client to an attorney for legal services performed on behalf of the client on an hourly basis without a written fee agreement?
conclusions: Justice Mary Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court held that the plain meaning of “account receivable” as used in Wash. Rev. Code 4.16.040(2) is an amount due to a business on account from a customer who has bought merchandise or received services. This plain meaning encompasses a balanced owed by a client to an attorney for legal services performed, even if on an hourly fee basis and without a written fee agreement. Since the balance incurred in the ordinary course of business, Tingey’s action is subject to the six-year limitation period applicable to actions under accounts receivable. Thus, the Court reversed the Court of Appeals decision and reinstated the trial court’s ruling on summary judgment that the six-year limitation period is applicable.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Dornay
facts: Petitioner Margita A. Dornay was charged for intentionally giving false testimony as a witness in a judicial proceeding by the Washington State Bar Association’s Disciplinary Board. Dornay admitted giving false testimony during a later hearing and in her deposition to the Washington State Bar Association. After weighing the aggravating factors against the mitigating factors, the Disciplinary Board concluded Dornay knowingly violated Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4 and §3.3 by giving false testimony, but did not commit perjury. The Board amended the hearing officer’s recommended sanction of a two-month suspension and unanimously agreed to a three-year suspension. Dornay appealed to the Supreme Court of Washington claiming the sanction was inappropriate considering she was under duress at the time of her testimony. The Board cross-appealed claiming it improperly weighed the aggravating and mitigating factors because the evidence does support a charge of perjury, and asserted Dornay should be disbarred.
questions: Did the Disciplinary Board err in finding Dornay failed to establish the defense of duress, as well as in finding a clear preponderance of the evidence did not support a charge of perjury but supported a charge of false swearing in violation of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4 and §3.3? Did the Board properly weigh the mitigating and aggravating factors when determining Dornay’s sanction?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court concluded that because Dornay admitted to giving false testimony, she cannot make any argument she did not knowingly make materially misleading statements under oath in a judicial proceeding. Thus, the Court agreed with the Disciplinary Board’s conclusion that Dornay’s duress defense was not supported and she knowingly violated Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §8.4 and §3.3. Because the Board was correct in its initial determination that the weight of the mitigating factors exceeded the weight of the aggravating factors, which subsequently led to finding a clear preponderance of evidence proving Dornay guilty of false swearing but not perjury, the Court upheld the three-year suspension.

title: State of Washington v. Thiefault
facts: Petitioner Gaylon Thiefault was convicted of attempted second degree rape in the Superior Court for Snohomish County. As Thiefault had three prior convictions, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole pursuant to Washington’s Persistent Offender Accountability Act (Washington Revised Code §9.94A). Thiefault appealed his sentence, asserting that he had received ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to object to the comparability of a previous conviction in Montana to a Washington “strike” offense. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Thiefault’s sentence. Thiefault appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Theifault receive ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to object to the comparability of his Montana conviction?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the offense Thiefault was convicted of in Montana requires a lesser mens rea than its Washington counterpart and as there is a reasonable probability that his attorney’s failure to object to the state’s comparability analysis prejudiced Thiefault, Thiefault received ineffective assistance of counsel. Thus, the Court remanded the case for resentencing.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Chenoweth
facts: Petitioners Randal Chenoweth and Barbara Wood motioned for the suppression of evidence used in their prosecution of unlawful manufacture of methamphetamine. Specifically, they argued the evidence of the crimes found on the property was obtained by a search warrant issued on the basis of uncorroborated information provided by a named informant. They challenged the validity of the search warrant, contending that the State omitted material facts concerning the known informant’s background in violation of the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution and Article I, Sect. 7 of the Washington Constitution. The Whitcom County Superior Court denied the motion, ruling that the Deputy Prosecuting Attorney who obtained the search warrant did not recklessly omit the material facts. On Appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment against Wood, and affirmed in part and reversed in part the judgment against Chenoweth, holding that any omissions or inaccuracies in the affidavit in support of the search warrant were innocent or negligent rather than intentional or reckless, and that the State Constitution does not allow challenges to search warrants based on negligent omissions. The Supreme Court of Washington granted the petition for review.
questions: Is a warrant valid under Article I, Sect. 7 of the Washington Constitution when a warrant affiant negligently fails to disclose facts that, if known, would have negated the probable cause determination of criminal offense?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the judgment in the Court of Appeals, holding that under Article I, Sect. 7 of the State Constitution material misstatements or omissions will invalidate a search warrant only when made recklessly or intentionally. The trial court’s conclusion that the prosecutor did not recklessly omit material facts in obtaining a search warrant was not clearly erroneous, and that the warrant contains adequate indicia of the informant’s reliability. The Court also affirmed the Court of Appeals finding that the second count of unlawful possession of a controlled substance against Chenoweth violated the prohibition of double jeopardy, and the Chenoweth case was remanded for resentencing.

title: Seto v. American Elevator, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Matthew Seto filed a civil suit against respondent American Elevator, Inc. in the Superior Court for King County. The case was subsequently transferred to arbitration. After hearing the case, the arbitrator returned a decision for the defense and mailed a copy of their decision to the attorneys for both parties. Twenty days after receiving the decision and twenty-one days after the decision was mailed, Seto petitioned the superior court for a trial de novo. American Elevator moved for Seto’s request to be set aside on grounds that Seto had not complied with Washington Revised Code §7.06.050(1)’s requirement that a party seeking a trial de novo must request one within twenty days of the filing of the arbitrator’s decision. The superior court granted the motion. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s ruling. Seto appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: When does §7.06.050(1)’s twenty day deadline for requesting a trial de novo begin to run?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case for trial, concluding that §7.06.050(1)’s twenty day deadline for requesting a trial de novo does not begin to run until service by mail of the arbitrator’s decision is complete. Thus, as Seto submitted his request within twenty days of receiving the arbitrator’s decision, his request was timely.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Kronich
facts: Petitioner Kyle Kronich was convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol and driving while his driver’s license was suspended in the District Court for Spokane County after a trial in which a certification from the Department of Licensing that Kronich’s driver’s license was suspended was admitted into evidence. Kronich appealed his conviction, asserting that the certification was hearsay and that its admission therefore violated his right under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution to be confronted with the witnesses against him. The Superior Court for Spokane County and the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Kronich’s conviction. Kronich petitioned the Supreme Court of Washington for review.
questions: Was the Department of Licensing’s certification evidence that was testimonial in nature and therefore inadmissible hearsay?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that public records such as the Department of Licensing’s certification are not testimonial in nature. Thus, the Court held that the state of Washington was not required to establish that the declarant is unavailable to testify or that the defendant had opportunity to cross examine the declarant and that the trial court did not err in admitting the certification into evidence.

title: State of Washington v. Coleman
facts: Petitioner John Coleman was convicted of two counts of child molestation arising from his alleged molestation of two children over a period of three years. Coleman subsequently appealed his convictions, asserting that the trial court erred in failing to include a unanimity instruction in its instructions to the jury.
