The Washington Court of Appeals reversed one of Coleman’s convictions but affirmed the other, holding that as the state of Washington had not emphasized specific incidents of molestation involving one of the alleged victims, a unanimous verdict on a specific criminal act was not required to convict Coleman of molesting her. Coleman appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court err in failing to instruct the jury that it needed to reach a unanimous verdict on a specific criminal act in order to convict Coleman? If so, was the error harmless?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the state introduced evidence of multiple distinguishable incidents of molestation, the trial court was required to instruct that jury that it needed to reach a unanimous verdict on a specific criminal act in order to convict Coleman to avoid the risk of jurors improperly aggregating evidence. The Court also held that this error was not harmless and therefore vacated Coleman’s conviction and remanded the case to the trial court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Kirkpatrick
facts: Petitioner Nathan Kirkpatrick was convicted of reckless driving and operating a motor vehicle without a valid operator’s license after a trial in which a certification from the Department of Licensing that Kirkpatrick does not have a driver’s license was admitted into evidence. Kirkpatrick appealed his conviction, asserting that the certification was hearsay and that its admission therefore violated his right under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution to be confronted with the witnesses against him. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Kirkpatrick’s conviction. Kirkpatrick appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the Department of Licensing’s certification evidence that was testimonial in nature and therefore inadmissible hearsay?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that just as a public record is not testimonial in nature, a certification of the absence of a public record is not testimonial in nature. Thus, the Court held that the state of Washington was not required to establish that the declarant is unavailable to testify or that the defendant had opportunity to cross examine the declarant and that the trial court did not err in admitting the certification into evidence.

title: State of Washington v. Evans
facts: Petitioner Danny Evans was convicted of the manufacture of a controlled substance and possession of a controlled substance with intent to deliver after methamphetamine and drug paraphernalia were found in a briefcase in Evans’ automobile. Evans appealed his conviction, asserting that the warrantless search of the briefcase was unlawful. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Evans’ conviction, holding that Evans relinquished any privacy interest that he had in the briefcase when he denied ownership of it to the police officer who conducted the search. Evans appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Evans’ denial of ownership of the briefcase relinquish his privacy interest in it?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Evans had a reasonable expectation of privacy in the contents of the briefcase and that his denial of ownership was by itself insufficient to relinquish this privacy interest. Thus, the Court held that the search was unlawful, reversed Evans’ conviction, and ordered the evidence derived from the search suppressed.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Nelson v. Appleway Chevrolet, Inc.
facts: Respondent Herbert Nelson purchased an automobile from petitioner Appleway Chevrolet, Inc. In addition to the agreed upon sale price, Appleway Chevrolet charged Nelson $79.23 to recoup the business and occupation tax that it owed as a result of the sale. Nelson subsequently filed a class action in the Superior Court for Spokane County requesting a declaratory judgment that Appleway Chevrolet’s attempt to shift its business and occupation tax burden onto its customers is unlawful. The superior court found for Nelson, ruling that Appleway Chevrolet’s policy violates Washington Revised Code §82.04.500. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the superior court’s ruling. Appleway Chevrolet appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §82.04.500 permit businesses to shift their business and occupation tax burden onto their customers?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the business and occupation tax imposed by §82.04.500 is a tax on businesses rather than on consumers and is part of businesses’ operating overhead. Thus, while a business may itemize the tax as part of the final purchase price, it may not add a business and occupation tax charge to the final purchase price.

title: State of Washington v. Watt
facts: Petitioner Kendra Watt was convicted of criminal mistreatment and the possession and manufacture of methamphetamine after a trial in which out of court statements made by her husband were admitted into evidence. Watt appealed her convictions, asserting that the admission of her husband’s out of court statements violated her right under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution to be confronted with the witnesses against her. The Washington Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court of Washington both affirmed Watt’s convictions. However, the United States Supreme Court vacated Watt’s convictions and remanded the case for reconsideration in light of its decision in Crawford v. Washington. The Washington Court of Appeals once again affirmed Watt’s convictions, holding that while the admission of Watt’s husband’s out of court statements violated Watt’s right to confrontation, the error was harmless as overwhelming evidence supported her convictions. Watt appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that under Crawford, violations of a defendant’s right to confrontation are not subject to harmless error analysis.
questions: Did the admission of her husband’s out of court statements violate Watt’s right to confrontation? If so, was the error harmless? If so, does Crawford nonetheless require automatic reversal?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that while the admission of Watt’s husband’s out of court statements violated Watt’s right to confrontation, the error was harmless as overwhelming evidence supported her convictions. The Court also held that Crawford does not require automatic reversal in cases in which a defendant’s right to confrontation has been violated.

title: United Collection Service, Inc. v. Shepherd
facts: American Discount Corporation assigned a judgment obtained against respondent Austin Shepherd and his wife Joy in 1986 to petitioner United Collection Service, Inc., which in 1996 obtained an order extending the judgment for ten years pursuant to Washington Revised Code §6.17.020. After United Collection Service subsequently moved to appoint an appraiser for the Shepherds’ real property upon which an execution had been levied, Shepherd moved to set aside the order extending the judgment as void. Shepherd cited J.D. Tan, L.L.C. v. Summers, in which the Washington Court of Appeals held that, prior to its 2002 amendment, §6.17.020 only authorized original creditors to obtain orders extending judgments. The superior court denied Shepherd’s motion and appointed an appraiser. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, ruling that as the version of §6.17.020 in effect in 1996 only authorized original creditors to obtain orders extending judgments, the judgment against Shepherd expired in 1996 after the ten year limit on judgment enforceability established by Washington Revised Code §4.56.210 expired. United Collection Service appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the order extending the judgment against Shepherd void under §6.17.020 at the time that it was issued? If so, did the 2002 amendment to §6.17.020, which authorizes both original creditors and assignees to obtain orders extending judgments, retroactively validate the 1996 extension?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the judgment against Shepherd had expired in 1996 insofar as the order extending the judgment was void given that the version of §6.17.020 in effect in 1996 only authorized original creditors to obtain orders extending judgments. The Court also held that the 2002 amendment to §6.17.020 did not retroactively validate the 1996 extension as reviving an expired judgment would affect a substantive right and retroactive statutes cannot affect substantive rights.

title: State of Washington v. Graham
facts: Richard Graham and Michele Cunliffe are divorced and share custody of their two children equally. After both Graham and Cunliffe’s income changed and one of the children moved into a new age category on the child support schedule, the state of Washington petitioned for modification of their parenting plan. In response, Graham petitioned to have his support payment modified pursuant to the support formula used in In re marriage of Arvey, a case that involved a parenting plan in which each parent had custody of one of two children. The commissioner for the Superior Court for King County declined to apply the Arvey support formula to cases in which parents share custody of their children equally and instead extrapolated Graham’s child support obligation from Washington Revised Code §26.19’s economic table, which does not calculate child support obligations for parents with monthly incomes in excess of $7,000. Graham appealed the commissioner’s decision, asserting that it imposed an inequitable burden upon him. The superior court reversed the commissioner’s decision and based its revision of Graham’s child support obligation upon the Arvey support formula. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the Arvey support formula is inapplicable to cases in which parents share custody of their children equally and that extrapolation of child support obligations from §26.19’s economic table is appropriate in cases in which a parent’s monthly income exceeds $7,000. Graham appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Arvey’s allocation of child support obligations applicable to cases in which parents share custody of their children equally? Does §26.19 permit extrapolation from its economic table in cases in which a parent’s monthly income exceeds $7,000?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals. The Court concluded that Arvey’s allocation of child support obligations is not applicable to cases in which parents share custody of their children equally. However, the Court also held that §26.19 does not permit extrapolation from its economic table in cases in which a parent’s monthly income exceeds $7,000 insofar as §26.19 requires that the amount of support be based upon the child or children’s specific needs.

title: State of Washington v. Hacheney
facts: Petitioner Nicholas Hacheney was convicted of first-degree premeditated murder for killing his wife in the course of arson, and was sentenced to life without the possibility of release under Wash. Rev. Code §10.95.020(11)(e). Hacheney appealed, arguing that the jury was improperly instructed on the aggravating factor and that there was insufficient evidence to show that he committed the murder in the course of arson because his wife was dead before he set fire to the house. He also argued the trial judge violated his Sixth Amendment right to confrontation by allowing the jury to view videotaped dispositions of three witnesses who were out of the country at the time of the trial. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Hacheney’s petition for review.
questions: Does the State’s evidence provide probable cause to support the charge that Hacheney committed the murder “in the course of” arson in the first degree? Did the State sufficiently establish the unavailability of the three witnesses to support admission of their videotaped disposition?
conclusions: Justice Bobbe Bridge’s opinion for the Court held that the evidence did not support a charge that Hacheney murdered his wife in the course of arson because the murder was complete before the arson and the murder did not further the arson as a matter of law. Thus, the Court reversed the Court of Appeals judgment in part and remanded for resentencing without consideration of the improper aggravating circumstance. As to the second issue, the Court affirmed in part the Court of Appeals judgment that Hacheney’s rights under the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause were not violated when the trial court admitted the witnesses’ videotaped depositions into evidence because the State sufficiently established that those witnesses were unavailable to testify in person at the trial.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: McCausland v. McCausland
facts: Petitioner Robert McCausland and his wife, respondent Angela McCausland, entered into a reconciliation agreement following their separation under which Robert McCausland agreed to pay his wife a monthly sum for spousal maintenance and child support. When Robert McCausland’s financial circumstances changed, he petitioned for termination of the spousal maintenance payments and modification of the child support payments. The trial court ruled that the reconciliation agreement is enforceable. Robert McCausland appealed, asserting that the trial court erred in extrapolating his child support obligation from Washington Revised Code §26.19’s economic table, which does not calculate child support obligations for parents with monthly incomes in excess of $7,000. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court, holding that §26.19 grants the trial court authority to extrapolate in cases in which a parent’s monthly income exceeds the range listed in the economic table. McCausland appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May a court extrapolate in calculating the child support obligation of a parent whose monthly income exceeds the range listed in §26.19’s economic table?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a court may not automatically extrapolate in calculating the child support obligation of a parent whose monthly income exceeds the range listed in §26.19’s economic table. While a court may nonetheless set a parent’s child support obligation at a level that exceeds the maximum amount provided for by the economic table, it must do so on the basis of written findings of fact justifying an extraordinary award. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Lord
facts: Respondent Brian Lord was convicted of first degree murder in the Superior Court for Kitsap County after a trial in which spectators were permitted to wear buttons bearing photos of the victim. Lord appealed his conviction, asserting that the buttons were inherently prejudicial and that the trial court erred in failing to remove them from the courtroom. Lord also asserted that the trial court erred in excluding the testimony of a bloodhound handler who tracked the victim’s scent following her disappearance insofar as this testimony would have contradicted the state of Washington’s theory of the crime. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Lord’s conviction. Lord appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Lord denied a fair trial by the buttons worn by spectators? Did the trial court err in excluding the testimony of the bloodhound handler on grounds that it would be irrelevant?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that silent displays of affiliation worn by spectators that do not explicitly advocate guilt or innocence are not inherently prejudicial. The Court also held that the trial court properly excluded the testimony of the bloodhound handler as this testimony would not have directly contradicted the state’s theory of the crime and is therefore irrelevant.

title: State of Washington v. Womac
facts: Petitioner Brian Womac was convicted of homicide by abuse, second degree felony murder, and first degree assault in the Superior Court for Pierce County. The trial court subsequently sentenced Womac to an exceptional sentence on the homicide by abuse conviction but did not sentence Womac on the second degree felony murder and first degree assault convictions in order to avoid subjecting him to double jeopardy. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed Womac’s exceptional sentence on grounds that it was based upon findings of fact made by the judge rather than by the jury. The Washington Court of Appeals also directed the trial court to conditionally dismiss Womac’s second degree felony murder and first degree assault convictions pending appellate review. Womac appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the second degree felony murder and first degree assault convictions subjected him to double jeopardy and should have been unconditionally dismissed.
questions: Did the trial court err in imposing an exceptional sentence on the basis of findings of fact made by the judge rather than by the jury? If so, was the error harmless? Did the trial court’s failure to dismiss Womac’s second degree felony murder and first degree assault convictions subject him to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals. The Court found that aggravating factors supporting an exceptional sentence must be submitted to the jury and proven beyond a reasonable doubt and that the trial court therefore erred in imposing an exceptional sentence. The Court also held that this error was not harmless as Washington law at the time of Womac’s trial contained no provision for a jury to be empanelled to make the necessary findings of fact. Consequently, the Court reversed Womac’s exceptional sentence and remanded the case for resentencing within the standard range, The Court also directed the trial court to dismiss Womac’s second degree felony murder and first degree assault convictions on remand, holding that convictions, even convictions for which no sentence is imposed, are punishments for purposes of double jeopardy. Thus, as all three of Womac’s convictions arose from the same criminal conduct, Womac was subjected to double jeopardy.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Mason
facts: Petitioner Kim Mason was convicted in the Superior Court for King County of murdering a man who had previously accused him of kidnapping and attempted murder in order to eliminate him as a witness. During his trial testimony was heard from witnesses who recounted statements the victim had made regarding seeking a protective order against Mason prior to his murder. Mason subsequently appealed his conviction and sentence to the Supreme Court of Washington, alleging that the admission of testimony from third parties regarding statements made by the victim violated his right to confront witnesses against him under the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
questions: Did Mason forfeit his right to confront the victim by making them unavailable as a witness by murdering them?
conclusions: Justice Chambers' opinion for the Court concluded that defendants lose their right to confront witnesses against them when there is clear, cogent, and convincing evidence that the unavailability of those witnesses is due to the defendant's own actions and that that standard had been met in Mason's case.

title: Department of Labor and Industries v. Granger
facts: Petitioner Department of Labor and Industries sought judicial review after the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals ordered the value from respondent William Granger’s employer-contributions into his medical benefit and health-care trust at the time he sustained an industrial injury should be entered into the worker’s monthly wage basis for calculating his time-loss compensation. The Department of Labor and Industries argued Granger was not eligible to receive the benefits from the trust at the time of his injury because he did not reach the minimum hours worked for the month of his injury according to the rules in his union’s “hour-bank system.” The Department of Labor and Industries appealed to the Skagit County Superior Court which affirmed the Board’s order to include the money Granger’s employer paid into the trust during wage calculation. The Department appealed to the Division One Court of Appeals which also affirmed the order. The Supreme Court of Washington granted the Department's petition for review.
questions: Should the payments an employer was making into an employee’s health care trust fund at the time of the employee’s injury be included in the wage calculation for time-loss compensation if the employee was not entitled to the benefits at the time?
conclusions: Justice Bobbe J. Bridge wrote the opinion for the court affirming the Court of Appeals, concluding that according to the language in Revised Code of Washington §51.08.178, the employer payments into a trust fund that provides health care coverage to a union member are “considerations of a like nature.” Furthermore, it is clear that “receiving at the time of injury” refers to the payment made for the benefit and not on eligibility itself. Because the employer made the contributions in the trust account in return for Granger’s work, the amount paid represents his earning capacity at the time of his injury and should properly be included in his wage basis for purposes of his time-loss compensation.

title: State of Washington v. Miles
facts: Petitioner Michael Miles was charged with securities fraud, witness intimidation and tampering, and theft. The charges were supported by evidence gathered by the Department of Financial Institutions’ Securities Division, which issued an administrative subpoena to Miles’ bank in the course of its investigation of allegations that Miles defrauded investors. The trial court denied Miles’ motion to suppress evidence derived from the search of his bank records, ruling that because Miles had a reduced expectation of privacy given his participation in the pervasively regulated securities industry, his right to privacy under Article I §7 of the Washington State Constitution had not been infringed by the Securities Division’s failure to notify him of the search. Miles appealed this ruling to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the Securities Division’s search of Miles’ bank records infringe his right to privacy under Article I §7?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court and ordered the evidence derived from the search of Miles’ bank records suppressed, concluding that Miles’ participation in the pervasively regulated securities industry does not expose his non-business related private matters to public inspection without a judicially issued search warrant or subpoena.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Kinney v. Cook
facts: Respondent Clark Kinney and petitioner Kenneth Cook formed a corporation that sold and serviced heavy duty trucks. Kinney eventually decided to sell his stock in the corporation to Cook and the parties signed a memorandum of understanding under which a debt owed to Cook by Kinney was cancelled in exchange for Kinney’s stock being transferred to Cook. Kinney subsequently filed suit against Cook in an effort to void this agreement, claiming that Cook had misrepresented the fair market value of the stock. Consequently, Cook was ordered to return the stock to Kinney and Kinney’s debt to Cook was reinstated. Following the judgment, Cook demanded payment on the debt and Kinney complied in exchange for the return of the stock. However, prior to the judgment, Cook had authorized the corporation to guarantee a large loan made by Mercedes Benz Credit Corporation to a limited liability corporation that Cook owns. When Kinney became aware of this loan, he filed suit against Cook, claiming that Cook’s actions violated Washington’s Securities Act (Washington Revised Code §21.20). The trial court granted summary judgment for Cook, ruling that the transaction between Kinney and Cook was not a sale of securities and that the Securities Act was therefore inapplicable. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the broad definition of sales of securities under the Securities Act and its liberal approach to providing relief for securities fraud victims made summary judgment inappropriate. Cook appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the court-ordered rescission of the agreement between Kinney and Cook a sale of securities for purposes of the Securities Act?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the judgment rescinding the agreement between Kinney and Cook merely restored the parties to their previous positions and did not give rise to a sale of securities. In particular, as Kinney already owned the stock at the time of his payment to Cook and as this payment was made in satisfaction of a preexisting debt rather than in consideration for an investment made at the time of payment, any fraud committed in inducing it did not fall within the scope of the Securities Act.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Burns v. Seattle
facts: Seattle City Light, the respondent city of Seattle’s municipal electric utility, entered into agreements with several adjacent cities in which it agreed to pay a percentage of the revenues it received from providing electricity to the cities’ residents to the cities in exchange for the cities’ promise to forbear from establishing their own municipal electric utilities. Petitioner Doris Burns subsequently petitioned for a declaratory judgment that the agreements are illegal insofar as they violate Washington Revised Code §35.21.860(1), which prohibits the imposition of franchise fees upon the light and power distribution business by cities and towns. The trial court granted summary judgment for the city of Seattle. Burns appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the payments provided for in the agreements between Seattle City Light and the cities constitute illegal franchise fees?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that the payments provided for in the agreements between Seattle City Light and the cities do not constitute franchise fees as they are not fees imposed for the right to use and occupy city streets enacted pursuant to the cities’ powers of taxation and regulation but rather consideration in exchange for the cities’ promise to forbear from entering into competition with Seattle City Light by establishing their own municipal electric utilities.

title: State of Washington v. Watson
facts: Petitioner Eric Watson was convicted of first degree child molestation. Upon his release from prison, he registered, as required by Washington Revised Code §9A.44.130, as a sex offender with the Pierce County Sheriff’s Department. Shortly thereafter, Watson was convicted of violating the terms of his community custody and spent an additional 60 days in jail. After he was released, Watson returned to his residence and did not re-register as a sex offender. The state of Washington subsequently charged him in the Superior Court for Pierce County with failing to register as a sex offender and Watson was found guilty and sentenced to 30 days in jail. Watson appealed his conviction, asserting that §9A.44.130 is unconstitutionally vague with regard to whether a sex offender is required to re-register when they return to the same residence after incarceration for a probation violation. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Watson’s conviction. Watson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Are the sex offender registration requirements of §9A.44.130 unconstitutionally vague?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although the language of §9A.44.130 is somewhat vague with regard to whether a sex offender is required to re-register when they return to the same residence after incarceration for a probation violation, it is not unconstitutionally vague. In particular, the Court held that case law, which is presumptively available to all citizens, clearly establishes that incarceration for a probation violation is the functional equivalent of incarceration for the original conviction for which probation was granted. Thus, as §9A.44.130 requires that sex offenders register as such once they complete their term of custody for a sex offense and are released into the community, Watson was required to re-register when he was released from jail.

title: Washington State Farm Bureau Federation v. Gregoire
facts: In 1993, the voters enacted the Taxpayer Protection Act (Washington Revised Code §43.135), which limits the growth of state expenditures and requires voter approval of any tax increase raising general fund revenues in excess of this limit, via initiative. Thirteen years later, the legislature amended §43.135 to raise the expenditure limit. In response, the Washington State Farm Bureau Federation petitioned for a declaratory judgment that tax increases subsequently enacted by the legislature to raise revenues in excess of the original limit established by §43.135 are invalid. The superior court granted summary judgment for the Washington State Farm Bureau Federation, ruling that the tax increases are invalid absent voter approval. Governor Christine Gregoire appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the taxes enacted by the legislature in excess of the original limits on state expenditures established by §43.135 require voter approval?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the superior court, concluding that the 2006 amendment to §43.135 is a valid legislative enactment that permits the legislature to raise revenue in excess of §43.135’s original limits on state expenditures without voter approval. In particular, as Article II §41 of the Washington State Constitution permits the legislature to amend any initiative two years after the voters enact it, the Court held that the amendment is lawful.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re Personal Restraint of Skylstad
facts: Petitioner Scott Skylstad filed a personal restraint petition (PRP) during the second of two direct appeals in the Washington Court of Appeals more than one year after his conviction of first degree robbery, but while his sentence was still on appeal. The Court of Appeals dismissed the PRP, holding that the petition to collaterally challenge the conviction was time-barred because the mandate issued in the first direct appeal affirming the conviction was the date of the final judgment, regardless if the sentence was still on appeal. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Skylstad’s petition for discretionary review of the PRP.
questions: Is a judgment final if a defendant’s sentence is still under appeal, even if the defendant’s conviction has been finalized?
conclusions: Justice Richard B. Sanders’ opinion for the Court concluded that Skylstad’s judgment was not final because his sentence was still being appealed. Pursuant to Wash. Rev. Code 10.73.090, a judgment becomes final when all litigation on the merits ends, and when review is terminated on both the sentence and the conviction. Since the trial court still had to determine Skylstad’s sentence, litigation on the merits continued and his judgment could not be final until his sentence was final. Furthermore, since his second appeal was still pending and no final judgment had been issued, the one-year limitation to file a PRP had not yet begun, so the Court of Appeals erred in holding Skylstad’s PRP time-barred. The Court remanded to the Court of Appeals to determine the merits of Skylstad’s PRP.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Anderson v. Department of Corrections
questions: Facts Petitioners Anderson and other life without parole (LWOP) inmates sought a declaration that a 20 percent deduction of non-work related income by respondent Department of Corrections was illegal and violated Wash. Rev. Code §72.09.480. The Department of Corrections claimed Wash. Rev. Code §72.11.020 granted it the authority to take such deductions and apply them toward court-ordered legal financial obligations (LFOs), so long as the deduction did not reduce the inmate's account below the established level of indigency. In addition, Wash. Rev. Code §72.11.030 established that court-ordered LFOs take priority over any other statutorily imposed mandatory withdrawals. The Challam County Superior Court agreed and ruled in favor of the Department of Corrections. The inmates appealed, and the Division Two Court of Appeals confirmed the trial court’s ruling. The inmates appealed again to the Supreme Court of Washington for review. Question(s) Does the Department of Corrections have the authority to impose LFO deductions on LWOF inmates’ non-work related income at its discretion? Does Wash. Rev. Code §72.09.480 supersede Wash. Rev. Codes §72.11.020 and .030? Conclusion Justice Bobbe J. Bridge's opinion for the Court affirmed the trial and Appeals court rulings, holding that Wash. Rev. Code §72.11.020 grants the Department of Corrections the authority to impose LFO deductions at its discretion, so long as the inmates balance remains above the level of indigency. Any other conclusion would allow LFOs on nonworking LWOP inmates to go unpaid and result in a conflict with legislative intent. In fulfilling the Court's obligation to reconcile statues when possible, the court declined to read Wash. Rev. Code §72.09.480 to supersede Wash. Rev. Codes §72.11.020 and .030, and the latter statutes provide that court-ordered LFOs hold priority over any other mandatory withdrawals from inmates’ accounts, even if Wash. Rev. Code §72.09.480 does not make such deductions mandatory.

title: State of Washington v. Conte
facts: Respondent John Conte was charged with violating Washington Revised Code §40.16.030, which prohibits knowingly offering any false or forged instrument to be filed, after he allegedly reimbursed several individuals for campaign contributions in order to conceal their source, thereby causing the recipients of those contributions to file false campaign finance disclosure forms. Conte successfully moved to dismiss the charges, asserting that the civil enforcement provisions of the Public Disclosure Act (Washington Revised Code §42.17) provide the exclusive penalties for the conduct alleged. The state of Washington appealed the trial court’s ruling. The Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §42.17 bar the state from prosecuting Conte under §40.16.030 for causing false campaign finance disclosure reports to be filed?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court, concluding that the civil enforcement provisions of §42.17 do not preempt §40.16.030 insofar as §42.17 expressly provides that it does not displace other remedies provided by law and insofar as there is no conflict between §42.17 and §40.16.030 given that one is a civil statute and the other a criminal statute. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the trial court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Yates
facts: After committing fifteen murders in four counties over the course of twenty years, petitioner Robert Yates was convicted of ten counts of first degree murder and one count of attempted first degree murder in the Superior Court for Spokane County and sentenced to 408 years in prison. Yates was also subsequently convicted of two counts of first degree murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County and sentenced to death. Yates appealed his convictions and sentence to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the Pierce County prosecuting attorney was equitably estopped from seeking the death penalty by his promise during plea negotiations between Yates and the Spokane County prosecuting attorney that he would not seek the death penalty. Yates also asserted that the trial court erred in excluding several prospective jurors who expressed opposition to the death penalty, that the prosecutor committed misconduct by making several prejudicial remarks during his trial, and that the jury’s decision to sentence him to death was supported by insufficient evidence and imposed a penalty disproportionate to that imposed in similar cases.
questions: Was the Pierce County prosecuting attorney equitably estopped from seeking the death penalty by their initial promise not to seek the death penalty? Did the trial court err in excluding several prospective jurors who expressed opposition to the death penalty? Did the prosecutor commit misconduct? If so, was the error harmless? Was the jury’s decision to sentence Yates to death supported by sufficient evidence? Is the death penalty a disproportionate penalty?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed Yates’ convictions and sentence, concluding that a defendant may not invoke equitable estoppel in order to obtain specific performance of an unwritten promise made in the context of plea negotiations. The Court also held that the trial court properly excluded several prospective jurors who expressed opposition to the death penalty on grounds that their beliefs would substantially impair the performance of their duties as jurors. Furthermore, although the prosecutor made a number of statements during Yates’ trial that were potentially improper, the Court found that these were not prejudicial. The Court also found that the decision to sentence Yates to death was supported by sufficient evidence insofar as substantial evidence supported the jury’s finding of insufficient mitigating circumstances to merit leniency. Finally, the Court held that the death penalty is not a disproportionate penalty in light of the penalties imposed in similar cases.

title: Udall v. T.D. Escrow Services, Inc.
facts: Lender U.S. Bancorp directed respondent T.D. Escrow Services, Inc. to commence foreclosure proceedings on a property after the borrower defaulted. T.D. Escrow Services proceeded to employ A.B.C. Legal Services to conduct the foreclosure sale. At the subsequent auction, petitioner William Udall was the high bidder and was given a receipt but not the deed of trust for the property. When T.D. Escrow Services discovered that A.B.C. Legal Services had erroneously sold the property to Udall at a price $100,000 lower than it had authorized, it refused to deliver the deed of trust to Udall. Udall responded by filing suit to quiet title. The trial court granted summary judgment for Udall. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the sale of the property had not been completed under the terms of Washington’s deed of trust act (Washington Revised Code §61.24) and that T.D. Escrow Services was therefore not required to deliver the deed of trust to Udall. Udall appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §61.24 require that a trustee deliver the deed of trust to the purchaser of a property following a foreclosure sale?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and ordered that title be quieted in Udall, concluding that under §61.24 a property is considered sold once the trustee accepts a bid unless there is a procedural irregularity that voids the sale. Thus, as deficiency in price alone is insufficient basis for setting aside a sale on grounds of procedural irregularity, the Court held that §61.24 requires that T.D. Escrow Services deliver the deed of trust to Udall.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Ohlson
facts: Petitioner James Ohlson was convicted of two counts of second degree assault in the Superior Court for Kitsap County after a trial in which one victim testified and the out of court statement of the other victim was admitted into evidence in lieu of their testimony. Ohlson appealed his conviction, asserting that the admission of the out of court statement infringed his right under the 6th Amendment to the United States Constitution to be confronted with the witnesses against him. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Ohlson’s conviction, holding that the out of court statement, which was made to a police officer arriving at the scene shortly after the assault, was an excited utterance and therefore non-testimonial in nature. Ohlson appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court infringe Ohlson’s right to be confronted with the witnesses against him by admitting the victim’s out of court statement into evidence?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although excited utterances are not necessarily non-testimonial in nature, the victim’s out of court statement, which was made to enable police assistance to meet an ongoing emergency, was non-testimonial and properly admitted.

title: Ehsani v. McCullough Family Partnership
facts: After a judgment in which respondent Sayed Zia Ehsani had to pay money into David C. Cullen’s client trust account, Cullen distributed the funds under his clients’ direction (petitioner McCullough Family Partnership) to the clients’ creditors, including himself for legal services rendered. Ehsani successfully appealed and the trial court’s judgment was reversed. On remand Ehsani filed a motion in King County Superior Court for restitution pursuant to Wash. RAP 12.8, asking the court to restore the funds Cullen previously distributed from his client trust account. The trial court denied the motion for restitution, and Ehsani appealed. The Division One Court of Appeals held that the trial court erred in denying Ehsani’s Wash. RAP 12.8 motion, and that Cullen is liable to Ehsani in restitution for the full amount since the funds were distributed from his client trust account. Cullen subsequently petitioned for review to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the case present the “appropriate circumstances” according to Wash. RAP 12.8 for post-appeal restitution? Did the trial court abuse its discretion in denying Eshani’s motion for restitution? Is Cullen liable to restore the funds that were dispersed from his client trust account?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson's opinion for the Court concluded that the Court of Appeals erred in its reversal of the trial court’s denial of Ehsani’s motion for restitution. According to the Wash. RAP 12.8, the case does not present the “appropriate circumstances” necessary for an award of restitution in which Cullen would be liable to restore the funds dispersed from his client trust account. Because of the vague language in Wash. RAP 12.8, the trial court had full discretionary authority to determine if the motion for restitution should be denied, and thus did not abuse it discretion. Cullen was a bone fide creditor of his clients and did not receive payments pursuant to a statutory scheme making him a real party of interest. Instead, Cullen was paid by the initial judgment creditors, his clients, for legal services rendered. The fact that these funds were held and distributed from Cullen’s client trust account does not alter this analysis, and thus he is not liable in restitution to Ehsani.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re Personal Restraint of Shale
facts: Petitioner Cole Shale pled guilty to three counts of first degree possession of stolen property and three counts of unlawful possession of payment instruments in the Superior Court for Spokane County. Shale subsequently moved to vacate his convictions and sentence on grounds that his offenses constitute a single unit of prosecution and that his offender score was improperly calculated. The superior court transferred the case to the Washington Court of Appeals for consideration as a personal restraint petition. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Shale’s convictions and sentence. Shale appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Shale’s multiple convictions subject him to double jeopardy in violation of the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution? Should Shale’s convictions have been treated as the “same criminal conduct” for purposes of calculating his offender score?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Shale’s plea agreement was an indivisible package agreement and that Shale cannot raise the double jeopardy issue without moving to withdraw all of his pleas. The Court also held that Shale cannot challenge the calculation of his offender score insofar as Shale failed to raise the factual issue of whether his convictions constitute the “same criminal conduct” prior to his sentencing.

title: State of Washington v. Benn
facts: Respondent Gary Benn was convicted of two counts of aggravated murder in the Superior Court for Pierce County. With regard to the presence of aggravating factors, the jury found that the murders were part of a common scheme or plan but did not return a verdict as to whether the murders were committed as a single act. Benn’s convictions were subsequently vacated on appeal and the state of Washington retried Benn. Benn was once again found guilty and the jury also found that the murders were committed as a single act. Consequently, Benn was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Benn appealed his sentence, asserting that he was subjected to double jeopardy when the state realleged the “single act” aggravating factor as the jury’s failure to return a verdict as to whether this aggravating factor was present in his first trial constituted an implied acquittal. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Benn’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Benn subjected to double jeopardy when the state retried the issue of whether the “single act” aggravating factor was present?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reinstated Benn’s sentence, concluding that double jeopardy principles do not apply to individual aggravating factors and that the jury’s failure to return a verdict as to whether the “single act” aggravating factor was present therefore did not constitute an acquittal for double jeopardy purposes.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Stewart-Graves v. Vaughn
facts: Petitioner Nichole Stewart-Graves’ son Liam was born without a heartbeat or spontaneous respiration but was eventually resuscitated by respondent Katherine Vaughn, the attending physician. However, due to the fact that he was not breathing for over twenty minutes before Vaughn succeeded in resuscitating him, Liam was left with severe brain damage and other disabilities. Stewart-Graves subsequently filed a medical malpractice action against Vaughn in the Superior Court for Clark County, asserting that Vaughn failed to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitation after ten minutes, at which point it was no longer reasonably possible for Liam to survive without severe brain damage, and that Vaughn breached the applicable standard of care by not discontinuing resuscitation at that point. The trial court granted summary judgment for Vaughn. Stewart-Graves appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Vaughn required to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitation of Liam Stewart-Graves after it was no longer reasonably possible for Liam to survive without severe brain damage? Did the applicable standard of care require that Vaughn discontinue resuscitation at that point?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that Vaughn was not required to obtain informed consent to continue resuscitating Liam Stewart-Graves as there was no opportunity for a deliberate and informed decision to refuse consent insofar as any delay would have resulted in Liam’s certain and immediate death. The Court also held that the applicable standard of care does not require a healthcare provider to withhold treatment of a newborn infant based upon the likelihood that the infant will be severely disabled if it survives.

title: State of Washington v. Day
facts: Petitioner Charlie Day was convicted of the manufacture of methamphetamine in the Superior Court for Benton County after a search of his automobile occasioned by it being illegally parked revealed evidence of methamphetamine manufacturing. Day appealed his conviction, asserting that the warrantless search of his automobile lacked probable cause. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Day’s conviction, holding that the search was based upon a reasonable suspicion that Day was engaged in criminal activity given that the police officer who found Day parked illegally noticed drug paraphernalia and an empty handgun case in Day’s automobile during their questioning of Day. Day appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May a police officer detain a suspect for questioning when their initial contact with the suspect arises from a parking infraction?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a police officer may not detain a suspect for questioning when they merely suspect a parking infraction. Thus, the Court ordered evidence derived from the search of Day’s automobile suppressed and remanded the case.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Carpenter
facts: Petitioner Timothy Carpenter was charged with two counts of misconduct by the Washington State Bar Association’s Disciplinary Board arising out of his representation of two codefendents in a lawsuit to collect on a property transaction. The Disciplinary Board recommended Carpenter be suspended from practicing law for two months for knowing violations of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7 and §1.9 for failing to withdraw when it became clear the codefendents had a conflict of interest, and §1.15(a) for representing one codefentent against the other in a later indemnification action without obtaining a consent or waiver allowing Carpenter’s involvement in the litigation. Carpenter appealed, claiming he acted out of negligence and the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction was inappropriate.
questions: Did Carpenter knowingly violate Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7 and §1.9 under the first charge, and §1.15(a) under the second charge? Is the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction appropriate after balancing the mitigating and aggravating factors?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for the Court upheld the Disciplinary Board’s recommended sanction, holding that Carpenter should have obtained a fully informed written consent from his former client allowing his involvement. The burden is on the attorney to do so when there is the possibility of conflicting interests, not on the client. Similarly, Carpenter had to undoubtedly know there was a conflict of interest between the codefendents, and should have withdrawn from representation. The Disciplinary Board correctly found that the aggravating factors of Carpenter’s legal experience, the multiple offenses involved, and the potential harm to the client, when weighed against the mitigating factors, provides substantial evidence to prove Carpenter committed knowing violations of Washington Rules of Professional Conduct §1.7, §1.9, and §1.15(a). The Court affirmed the Disciplinary Board’s recommendation of a two month suspension.

title: Potter v. Washington State Patrol
facts: After he was found driving with a suspended driver’s license, petitioner Mark Potter’s automobile was impounded by the respondent Washington State Patrol pursuant to the mandatory impoundment policy established by Washington Administrative Code §204-96-010. Following the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in All Around Underground, Inc. v. Washington State Patrol, in which the Court held that §204-96-010 is an unlawful exercise of the statutory authority granted to the Washington State Patrol in Washington Revised Code §46.55.113, Potter filed a class action lawsuit against the Washington State Patrol on behalf of himself and all of the owners of automobiles impounded pursuant to §204-96-010. The trial court granted summary judgment for the Washington State Patrol, ruling that an action for conversion cannot be brought against the Washington State Patrol insofar as its actions were authorized by law and reasonable. Potter appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the Washington State Patrol be held liable for conversion for impoundments carried out under the authority of §204-96-010 prior to the Supreme Court of Washington’s decision in All Around Underground, Inc. v. Washington State Patrol?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court and remanded the case, concluding that while the fact that the Washington State Patrol’s actions were authorized by law and reasonable immunizes its officers from liability, it does not immunize the Washington State Patrol as an organization from liability for promulgating a regulation that exceeded its statutory authority.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Woods v. Kittitas County
facts: Petitioner Cecile Woods filed suit against respondent Kittitas County in the Superior Court for Kittitas County pursuant to the Land Use Petition Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70C). Woods sought the reversal of the Kittitas County Commission’s decision to rezone a parcel of land from forest and range to rural. The superior court granted the petition and reversed the rezone, ruling that it was inconsistent with the Growth Management Act (Washington Revised Code §36.70A). Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the superior court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act. Woods appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the superior court have jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a Land Use Petition Act challenge to a site-specific land use decision can only be for violations of a comprehensive plan or for violations of development regulations and that the superior court therefore lacked jurisdiction to decide whether the rezone is consistent with the Growth Management Act. Turning to the remaining issues raised by Woods, the Court held that the rezone was supported by substantial evidence and was not based upon an erroneous interpretation of the law or a clearly erroneous application of the law to the facts.

title: State of Washington v. Daniels
facts: Respondent Carissa Daniels was charged with homicide by abuse and second degree murder after her son died in her care. The jury subsequently found Daniels guilty of second degree murder but left the verdict form pertaining to the homicide by abuse charge blank. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed Daniels’ conviction on grounds that assault cannot be a predicate offense for second degree murder. The Washington Court of Appeals also held that the state of Washington may not retry Daniels for homicide by abuse insofar as the jury’s silence on that charge acted as an implied acquittal. The state of Washington appealed this part of the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision to the Supreme Court of Washington. Daniels cross-petitioned, asserting that retrying her for second degree murder would subject her to double jeopardy.
questions: Was the jury’s silence on the charge of homicide by abuse an implied acquittal? Would retrying Daniels for second degree murder subject her to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the jury’s silence on the charge of homicide by abuse was not an implied acquittal insofar as the jury was instructed to leave the verdict form pertaining to homicide by abuse blank only if it was unable to agree. The Court also held that retrying Daniels for second degree murder would not subject her to double jeopardy insofar as constitutional prohibitions against double jeopardy only bar the state from retrying defendants whose convictions have been reversed when the reason for reversal was insufficient evidence.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re Dependency of A.K.
facts: Petitioner A.K., a dependent child that had been placed in foster care, ran away from her foster home on several occasions. At the behest of the respondent Department of Social and Health Services, the Yakima County Juvenile Court exercised its inherent contempt power and sentenced A.K. to a period of detention in excess of that provided for by the juvenile contempt statute. A.K. appealed the juvenile court’s sanction to the Superior Court for Yakima County and the Washington Court of Appeals, both of which upheld the sanction. A.K. appealed the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the juvenile court err in failing to consider the adequacy of statutory criminal contempt sanctions prior to exercising its inherent contempt power?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and vacated the sanction imposed by the juvenile court, concluding that the statutory criminal contempt sanctions provided for by Washington Revised Code §7.21.040 may be imposed to sanction violations of a dependency order and that the juvenile court erred in failing to consider the adequacy of these sanctions prior to exercising its inherent contempt power.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Olver v. Fowler
facts: Petitioner Julie Fowler and Respondent Michael Olver were appointed special administrators of the estates of a couple involved in a committed intimate relationship after both partners died in a traffic accident. Since the couple was not legally married, there was contention on how the shared assets would be divided. After a court order for binding mediation, the mediator concluded that even though majority of the assets were in the male partner’s name, the female partner was entitled to 50 percent of his assets and ordered the transfer. The day before presentation to the Superior Court for King County a father to one of the children who survived the accident was granted a motion to intervene, contesting the law does not allow application of meretricious relationship doctrine (law of committed intimate relationships) where both partners are deceased. Furthermore, he argued if the doctrine did apply, the surviving child would be unjustly shielded from gaining access to the male partner’s assets if she prevailed in her liability claim. The Superior Court ordered 50 percent of the male’s assets be disbursed to the female’s estate, and explained the legal effect of a committed intimate partner relationship upon a tort creditor’s claim should be determined in the context of the liability case. Petitioner Fowler, administrator of the male partner’s estate, joined with the father in the appeal of the trial court’s judgment. Respondent Olver, administrator of the female partner’s estate, cross-appealed arguing the trial court erred in granting the father’s motion to intervene. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Fowler’s petition for review.
questions: Did the trial court abuse its discretion when it allowed a party asserting a tort claim against a couple’s property to intervene in an action between their estates? Can Washington’s law of meretricious or committed intimated relationships be applied where both partners are deceased? Can tort claims against one committed intimate partner be made against the other partner’s estate under a theory of joint tort liability?
conclusions: Justice Bobbe J. Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the judgments and findings of both the trial court and the Court of Appeals. Specifically, that the trial court did not abuse its discretion when granting intervention to the father, and that Washington’s law of committed intimate relationships can be applied to divided assets between committed partners’ estates where both partners are deceased. Finally, since neither of the lower courts addressed the principles of joint tort liability being extended to committed intimate partners in this case, and instead concluded resolution of the issue is best for a separate suit filed against the female’s estate, the Court also declined to address the issue.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Department of Corrections v. Fluor Daniel, Inc.
facts: After a dispute arose between petitioner Fluor Daniel, Inc. and the respondent Department of Corrections regarding the terms of a contract to construct a prison, both parties agreed to binding arbitration. The arbitrator subsequently found in favor of Fluor Daniel and awarded it $5,997,645. Fluor Daniel submitted the decision to the Superior Court for King County for the entry of a judgment and also requested an award of pre-judgment interest for the period that elapsed between the arbitration and the judgment. The superior court granted Fluor Daniel’s request and awarded it pre-judgment interest, ruling that because the arbitrator’s decision could not be appealed, the damages awarded were fixed and interest began to accrue. The Department of Corrections appealed the award of pre-judgment interest and the Washington Court of Appeals reversed. Fluor Daniel appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the prevaling party in a binding arbitration entitled to pre-judgment interest for the period between the arbitration and the entry of a judgment?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that unless the parties’ arbitration agreement states otherwise, interest does not accrue in the period between the arbitration and the entry of a judgment regardless of the finality of the arbitration.

title: In re disability proceeding against Keefe
facts: The respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board initiated a disciplinary proceeding against petitioner John Keefe after Keefe allegedly failed to comply with court rules and failed to avoid a conflict of interest. Keefe represented himself at the subsequent hearing and conducted his defense in a manner that suggested that a lack of mental capacity. In particular, Keefe made a number of statements that reflected delusional and paranoid thinking and a lack of grasp of reality. As a result, the disciplinary board initiated a supplemental disability proceeding and suspended the disciplinary proceeding. After hearing testimony from a psychiatric expert who concluded that Keefe likely suffers from paranoid schizophrenia, the disciplinary board recommended that Keefe be suspended and transferred to disability inactive status, finding that Keefe’s mental state renders him incapable of practicing law. Keefe appealed the disciplinary board’s finding and recommendation, asserting that they were supported by insufficient evidence.
questions: Does substantial evidence support the disciplinary board’s finding that Keefe’s mental state renders him incapable of practicing law?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the disciplinary board’s finding and recommendation, concluding that the psychiatric expert’s conclusion that Keefe likely suffers from paranoid schizophrenia had a reasonable basis despite the fact that the psychiatric expert was unable to personally examine Keefe. The Court also held that the disciplinary board could reasonably find this mental disability renders Keefe incapable of practicing law. Thus, the Court ordered Keefe suspended and transferred to disability inactive status.

title: State of Washington v. Frost
facts: Petitioner Joshua Frost was found guilty in King County Superior Court of six counts of robbery, one count of burglary, one count of attempted robbery, and two counts of assault for acting as a driver in several robberies. Frost appealed his convictions claiming the State showed prosecutorial vindictiveness, erroneous admission of his statements, and erroneous limitation of defense counsel’s closing argument that the state failed to meet its burden of proof as to any of the robbery offenses, and instead limited to arguing defense of duress. The Division One Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment and rejected all of Frost’s claims. The Supreme Court of Washington granted review only on the issue of the trial court’s limitation of defense counsel’s closing argument.
questions: Did the trial court abuse its discretion by limiting the defense counsel’s closing argument to defense of duress, thus infringing on Frost’s Sixth Amendment right to counsel and his Fourteenth Amendment right to due process of law?
conclusions: Justice James Johnson’s opinion for the Court held that Frost’s constitutional rights to counsel and due process of law were violated when the trial court prevented his defense counsel from arguing in closing both that the State failed to prove accomplice liability as to the robbery counts and that Frost participated in the robberies under duress. However, the trial court’s abuse of its discretion did not taint the evidence before the jury as counsel’s argument was not evidence, and the jury was properly instructed on the State’s burden of proof in establishing accomplice liability. Thus, the Court affirmed Frost’s conviction concluding beyond a reasonable doubt that any reasonable jury would have convicted Frost even absent the trial court’s limitation on defense counsel’s arguments.

title: State of Washington v. George
facts: Petitioner Keith George was convicted on two counts of violating a no-contact order from which the charges originated separately in Renton and Kent municipal courts, but were tried together in King County Superior Court. George argued that the Renton court erred in resetting the time for trial after he failed to appear to two pretrial hearings because he was detained by the city of Kent and King County Disctict Court on unrelated charges. He also argued that his conviction on the charge initially violated the prohibition against double jeopardy because the Kent municipal court had dismissed the charge with prejudice before it was tried in Superior Court. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, holding George’s right to a timely trial was not violated. The Supreme Court of Washington granted George’s petition for review.
questions: Must the State demonstrate it exercised good faith and due diligence in attempting to procure a defendant’s presence in court in order to avail itself of CrRLJ 3.3(c)(2)(ii), which requires a trial court to reset the time for trial when a defendant failed to appear at a proceeding?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court held that the application of CrRLJ 3.3(c)(2)(ii) does not require due diligence on the part of the State. However, the Renton municipal court improperly reset the time for trial clock because the period George was detained on unrelated charges is treated as an exclusion from the time for trial calculation and not a “failure to appear.” Affirming the judgment by the Court of Appeals, the Court also held that the trial was within the applicable time for trial period, and that George was not placed in double jeopardy when the second charge was dismissed with prejudice.

title: In re Personal Restraint of Bowman
facts: Petitioner Jacob Bowman was convicted of second degree felony murder with the predicate crime of drive-by shooting. Bowman subsequently filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that just as assault cannot serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder insofar as the assault is not independent of the murder, drive-by shooting cannot serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder insofar as the drive-by shooting is inextricably intertwined with the murder. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bowman’s conviction. Bowman appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May the crime of drive-by shooting serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as the crime of drive-by shooting is unlike the crime of assault in that it does not require a victim, only reckless conduct that creates a risk that a person may be injured, it is independent of the crime of murder and therefore may serve as a predicate crime to second degree felony murder.

title: State of Washington v. Posey
facts: Petitioner Daniel Posey was charged with first degree assault and second degree rape. Although Posey was a minor at the time, the juvenile court was required to decline jurisdiction because first degree assault is a “serious violent offense” under Washington Revised Code §13.04.030. Following a trial in adult criminal court, Posey was acquitted of first degree assault but convicted of second degree rape and sentenced. Posey appealed, asserting that the trial court lacked the authority to sentence him insofar as he had been acquitted of the charge upon which its jurisdiction was based. Posey also asserted that the trial court erred in excluding from evidence an email written by the alleged victim in which she indicated that she would enjoy being subjected to sexual violence. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Posey’s conviction and sentence. Posey appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court have the authority to sentence Posey for second degree rape after he was acquitted of the first degree assault charge that led the juvenile court to decline jurisdiction? Did the trial court err in excluding the alleged victim’s email from evidence under Washington’s “rape shield” law (Washington Revised Code §9A.44.020)?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed in part and reversed in part the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the case should have been remanded to the juvenile court once Posey was acquitted of first degree assault. However, the Court also held that the trial court did not err in excluding the alleged victim’s email from evidence given that it was not addressed to Posey and merely discussed potential sexual behavior.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Chhom
facts: While depositions of the charges against petitioners Chhom and Steever were pending under separate prosecutions, they were transported to a jail in Yakima County to serve sentences for misdemeanor convictions in municipal courts located in King County where the charges were filed. The jail services were provided to the municipal courts by Yakima County pursuant to the terms of an interlocal agreement. In both cases, the King County District Courts entered a judgment dismissing the prosecutions for violation of the time for trial rule. The Superior Court for King County affirmed the judgment for dismissal in the Steever case, but reversed the judgment in the Chhom case and reinstated the prosecution. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the Superior Court’s judgment in the Chhom case and reversed and remanded the judgment in the Steever case, holding that the time for trial period was not tolled while Steever was incarcerated in Yakima county. The cases were consolidated and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Chhom and Steever’s petition for discretionary review.
questions: Is a defendant detained “outside the county” for purposes of former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5)(1995)(tolling the time for trial) when serving a sentence imposed by a court of limited jurisdiction within the charging county in a detention facility located outside the county?
conclusions: Justice Barbara Madsen’s opinion for the Court reversed the judgments by the Court of Appeals, holding in agreement with the District Courts’ rulings that a defendant is not held “outside the county” within the meaning of former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5) when the defendant is sent outside the county to serve a sentence imposed by a court of limited jurisdiction within the county. The Court of Appeals erred in its interpretation of the provision when it considered the words “detained…outside the county” in isolation and referring solely to the geographical location of the detention facility. If read as a whole, it is apparent that former CrRLJ 3.3(g)(5) applies to circumstances when the defendant is under “foreign” jurisdiction. Thus, the rule for tolling the time for trial does not apply because Chhom and Steever were not detained “outside the county” while their charges were pending because they were under the supervision of courts within King County.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re Detention of Ambers
facts: Pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09, petitioner Kevin Ambers petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released from his civil commitment as a sexually violent predator. In support of the petition, Ambers submitted a report and declaration from an expert in the field of sex offender treatment that estimated that, if released, he has a 36% likelihood of reoffending over a fifteen year period. The superior court ruled that Ambers failed to present a prima facie case for release. In particular, the superior court found that although the expert’s report constituted evidence of a change in condition, the 2005 amendments to §71.09 require that a sexually violent predator seeking unconditional release present evidence indicating not only that their condition has changed but also that they are safe to be at large in the community. Ambers appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the 2005 amendments to §71.09 impose a higher threshold of proof for sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the superior court, concluding that the 2005 amendments to §71.09 were not intended to impose a higher threshold of proof for sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release. Instead, the Court held that the amended version of §71.09 continues to require merely that sexually violent predators seeking unconditional release present evidence indicating that they no longer meet the definition of a sexually violent predator. Thus, as the report and declaration submitted by Ambers indicates that he no longer meets the definition of a sexually violent predator, the Court found that Ambers is entitled to a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Bennett
facts: Petitioner Bruce Bennett was convicted of first degree escape in the Superior Court for Clallam County. Bennett subsequently appealed his conviction, asserting that the instruction given to the jury regarding the burden of proof, which was first used in the case of Washington v. Castle, denied him due process insofar as it undermined the presumption of innocence. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bennett’s conviction. Bennett appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the Castle instruction satisfy the minimum constitutional requirements of due process?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although language in the Castle instruction instructing the jury that “the law does not require proof that overcomes every possible doubt” and that it should find the defendant not guilty if it believes that there is a “real possibility” of their innocence is problematic, the instruction does not impermissibly shift the burden of proof. However, although the Court held that the Castle instruction satisfies the minimum constitutional requirements of due process, it instructed trial courts to henceforth use the standard Washington Pattern Jury Instruction.

title: Arkison v. Ethan Allen, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Arkison was the court-appointed chapter 7 bankruptcy trustee for Michelle Carter, who was injured in 2002 from a piece of furniture during the moving process by employees of a furniture moving company hired by respondent Ethan Allen Home Interiors. When Carter filed for chapter 7 bankruptcy that same year, she did not list the potential legal claim against Ethan Allen as an asset, and Arkison’s file to discharge Carter’s debts was accepted by the bankruptcy court and the case was closed. Three years later Carter filed the suit against Ethan Allen in King County Superior Court for the 2002 injury. Ethan Allen subsequently filed a motion for summary judgment arguing that judicial estoppel barred Carter’s claim on the basis of her failure to disclose the potential claim as an asset during her file for bankruptcy. The case was reopened, and Arkison argued Ethan Allen’s summary judgment claim could not use the judicial estoppel defense against a bankruptcy trustee, and moved to substitute himself as the real party of interest.
