The Superior Court granted Arkison real party of interest, but also granted Ethan Allen’s summary judgment against Arkison based on the judicial estoppel defense, thus dismissing the legal claim. After being denied the motion for reconsideration, The Supreme Court of Washington granted Arkison’s petition for direct review.
questions: May a trial court apply the doctrine of judicial estoppel against a bankruptcy trustee standing as the real party of interest?
conclusions: Justice Susan Owens' opinion for the Court concluded that a trial court may not generally apply the doctrine of judicial estoppel to bar a bankruptcy trustee standing as a real party from pursuing a debtor’s legal claim not listed as an asset in bankruptcy proceedings. The court has previously established that a bankruptcy trustee has a separate identity from the bankruptcy debtor, and thus cannot be judicially estopped based on inconsistent positions. The trial court thus abused its discretion, and the Supreme Court of Washington reversed the judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Armendariz
facts: Petitioner Ismael Armendariz was convicted of third degree assault and violating a no contact order in the Superior Court for King County and sentenced to five months in jail to be followed by one year of community custody. The trial court also ordered that Armendariz have no contact with the victim for five years, the statutory maximum term for third degree assault. Armendariz appealed the no contact order, asserting that the trial court lacked authority under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.505(8), which authorizes courts to impose crime-related prohibitions and affirmative conditions, to impose a no contact order effective for the statutory maximum term for his third degree assault conviction. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Armendariz’s sentence. Armendariz appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §9.94A.505(8) authorize a court to impose a no contact order as a crime-related prohibition effective for the statutory maximum term for the predicate crime?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although §9.94A.505(8), unlike the provision that it replaced (former Washington Revised Code §9.94A.120(20)), does not expressly provide that a court may impose crime-related prohibitions effective for the statutory maximum term for the predicate crime, the legislative history of §9.94A.505(8) indicates that the legislature did not intend to effect any substantive changes to §9.94A.120(20).

title: State of Washington v. Recuenco
questions: Is imposing a firearm sentence enhancement based on a deadly weapon finding subject to harmless error analysis under Washington law, and if so, was the error in this case harmless?

title: State of Washington v. Boyd
facts: Petitioner Michael Boyd was charged with possession of child pornography in the Superior Court for Pierce County. Boyd’s computer, which allegedly contains tens of thousands of images of child pornography, was seized as evidence. Prior to trial, Boyd moved to compel the state of Washington to provide him with a copy of the computer’s hard drive to enable independent testing. The trial court denied the motion, ruling that Boyd only has a right to reasonable access and entering an order that Boyd’s attorney be granted limited access to a copy of the hard drive in a state facility. Boyd appealed the trial court’s order directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Washington Criminal Rule 4.7 require that Boyd be provided with a copy of the computer’s hard drive?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the trial court’s order, concluding that Washington Criminal Rule 4.7 obliges the state to provide Boyd with a copy of the computer’s hard drive as a necessary consequence of Boyd’s right to effective representation and a fair trial. In particular, the Court held that given the nature of the evidence, effective representation requires a full and independent analysis of the computer’s hard drive and the images contained therein, which would not be possible under the constraints imposed by the trial court.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Nichols
facts: Petitioner Caleb Nichols was convicted of possession of methamphetamine in the Superior Court for Spokane County after a search of his person following a traffic stop revealed methamphetamine. Nichols appealed his conviction, asserting that the traffic stop was pretextual and that he had received ineffective assistance of counsel when his attorney failed to challenge its legality. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Nichols’ conviction. Nichols appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Nichols’ attorney ineffective in failing to challenge the legality of the traffic stop that led to the discovery of the methamphetamine on Nichols’ person?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Nichols’ attorney was not ineffective in failing to challenge the legality of the traffic stop insofar as the stop was not pretextual. In particular, although the police officer that made the stop noted that the automobile was being driven in a suspicious manner, the immediate reason for the stop was the driver’s commission of several traffic violations.

title: In re Personal Restraint of Mulholland
facts: Respondent Daniel Mulholland was convicted of six counts of first degree assault while armed with a firearm and one count of drive-by shooting in the Superior Court for Pierce County. The trial court ordered that Mulholland’s first degree assault sentences be served consecutively, ruling that under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.589(1)(b) it had no discretion to order that these sentences be served concurrently. After exhausting his direct appeals, Mulholland filed a personal restraint petition in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that the trial court erred in ruling that it lacked discretion to order that his first degree assault sentences be served concurrently. The Washington Court of Appeals vacated Mulholland’s sentence and remanded the case for resentencing, holding that the trial court misinterpreted the law and could have ordered that Mulholland serve his first degree assault sentences concurrently. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does a sentencing court have discretion to order that sentences for separate violent offenses be served concurrently as an exceptional sentence? If so, was the trial court’s misinterpretation of the law a fundamental defect that inherently results in a complete miscarriage of justice?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although §9.94A.589(1)(b) requires that sentences for serious violent offenses be served consecutively, a sentencing court may order that such sentences be served concurrently as an exceptional sentence imposed pursuant to Washington Revised Code §9.94A.535 if it finds that mitigating circumstances are present. The Court also held that Mulholland demonstrated, as a petitioner seeking to obtain relief on collateral review must, that the trial court’s misinterpretation of the law was a fundamental defect that inherently results in a complete miscarriage of justice.

title: Crafts v. Pitts
facts: Petitioner David Pitts entered into a contract with Glen Cloninger to convey his interest in a parcel of land that he was leasing to Cloninger if Pitts either defaulted on the lease or the lease expired before Pitts exercised his option to purchase. The lease subsequently expired without Pitts either renewing his lease or purchasing the property but Pitts refused to convey his interest in the property to Cloninger. After Cloninger assigned his interest in the property to respondent Gordon Crafts and his wife Jaymie, the Crafts filed suit against Pitts for specific performance. However, Pitts had in the interim declared bankruptcy and had his debts discharged by the bankruptcy court. The trial court ruled that the bankruptcy court had not discharged the Crafts’ action for specific performance and ordered Pitts to quitclaim the property. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s decision. Pitts appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was the Crafts’ action for specific performance discharged in Pitts’ bankruptcy?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the Crafts’ action for specific performance was not discharged in Pitts’ bankruptcy insofar as an alternative right to monetary damages could not compensate them for the loss of a unique parcel of land.

title: Spokane School District #81 v. Cowles Publishing Company
facts: Nathan Walters died as the result of an allergic reaction to a peanut butter cookie served to him as part of a school lunch on a field trip sponsored by the respondent Spokane School District #81. After Walters’ parents indicated their intent to file a wrongful death claim, they and the school district reached a settlement. In the interim, the Spokesman-Review, a newspaper owned by petitioner Cowles Publishing Company, submitted a request pursuant to the Public Records Act (Washington Revised Code §42.56) for all records related to the school district’s investigation and possible settlement of Nathan Walters’ death. The school district denied the request on grounds that the requested records are privileged communications and attorney work product and therefore exempt from disclosure under §42.56. The school district then requested a declaratory judgment that the records are exempt from disclosure while the Spokesman-Review moved for an order to
questions: Are the requested records privileged communications and attorney work product and therefore exempt from disclosure under §42.56? May a state agency seek a declaratory judgment as to whether a requested public record is subject to disclosure?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the requested records are exempt from disclosure under §42.56 insofar as they were relevant to a controversy to which the school district was a party and would not have been available under the rules of pretrial discovery because they were protected either by the work product doctrine or because they reflected privileged attorney-client communications. The Court also held that §42.56 allows a state agency to seek a declaratory judgment as to whether requested public record is subject to disclosure.

title: In re Personal Restraint of McCarthy
facts: Respondent Donald McCarthy was convicted of third degree assault with sexual motivation and sentenced to a minimum term of twelve months imprisonment and a maximum term of sixty months imprisonment. Prior to the expiration of McCarthy’s minimum sentence, the Indeterminate Sentence Review Board conducted a hearing pursuant to Washington Revised Code §9.95.420(3) to decide if he is eligible for release. After denying McCarthy’s request to be represented by an attorney, the board found that McCarthy is more likely than not to commit another sex offense if released and added twenty-four months to McCarthy’s minimum term. McCarthy subsequently filed a personal restraint petition seeking review of the board’s decision in the Washington Court of Appeals. It asserted that offenders have a right to counsel during hearings conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3). The Washington Court of Appeals held that due process requires that the board decide on a case by case basis whether offenders are entitled to counsel to ensure fundamental fairness. The state of Washington appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do offenders have a right to counsel during hearings conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3)?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that while offenders have a liberty interest at stake during a hearing conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3) and therefore are entitled to minimum due process, this does not include a right to counsel. In particular, the Court held that a hearing conducted pursuant to §9.95.420(3) is analogous to a parole hearing and has adequate safeguards against serious risk of error.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Everybodytalksabout
facts: Petitioner Darrell Everybodytalksabout was convicted of first and second degree felony murder in the Superior Court for King County. Prior to his sentencing, an employee of the Department of Corrections interviewed Everybodytalksabout as part of her preparation of the presentence investigation report. After Everybodytalksabout was sentenced to life in prison, he appealed his conviction, which was ultimately reversed on grounds that the trial court erred in admitting certain evidence. Upon retrial, the trial court admitted testimony by the Department of Corrections employee regarding incriminating statements Everybodytalksabout made during the interview. After he was once again found guilty, Everybodytalksabout appealed his conviction, asserting that as his attorney was not present during the interview and as he had not been informed of his Miranda rights, he had been denied his right to counsel and testimony regarding the incriminating statements that he made during the interview should therefore not have been admitted. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Everybodytalksabout’s conviction, holding that Everybodytalksabout had not been denied his right to counsel insofar as the Department of Corrections employee had not deliberately elicited the incriminating statements during the interview. Everybodytalksabout appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Everybodytalksabout denied his right to counsel when he was interviewed by the Department of Corrections employee without his attorney being present and without being informed of his Miranda rights?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Everybodytalksabout was denied his right to counsel when his attorney was not present during the interview and he was not informed of his Miranda rights insofar as the interview was conducted for the purpose of preparing the presentence investigation report and therefore represented a critical stage of the proceedings and insofar as the Department of Correction employee conducting the interview deliberately elicited Everybodytalksabout’s incriminating statements. Thus, the Court reversed Everybodytalksabout’s conviction and remanded the case.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Bergstrom
facts: Petitioner Gordon Bergstrom was convicted of first degree unlawful possession of a firearm in the Superior Court for King County. At a subsequent sentencing hearing to determine whether Bergstrom should be placed on electronic home monitoring, Bergstrom argued pro se that the state of Washington had miscalculated his offender score insofar as some of his prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct. After Bergstrom’s motion for a continuance to present evidence that his convictions arose from the same criminal conduct was denied, the trial court proceeded to sentence Bergstrom. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Bergstrom’s conviction but remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing and ordered that each party be allowed to present additional evidence regarding whether Bergstrom’s prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct. Bergstrom appealed the part of the Washington Court of Appeals’ decision that ordered that the state be allowed to present additional evidence at resentencing.
questions: Did Bergstrom’s pro se argument that some of his prior convictions arose from the same criminal conduct constitute a specific objection to the calculation of his offender score that placed the state on notice that it needed to present evidence?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Bergstrom’s pro se argument was not a specific objection insofar as Bergstrom’s attorney did not object the state’s calculation of his offender score either in their pre-sentence report or at the sentencing hearing. Thus, the Court held that the state was not on notice that it needed to present evidence and that the trial court erred in failing to order an evidentiary hearing at which both parties would be allowed to present additional evidence.

title: State of Washington v. Dion
questions: Did the juvenile court properly extend its jurisdiction beyond the defendant's 18th birthday?

title: Sherry v. Financial Indemnity Company
facts: Respondent Kevin Sherry was injured by an uninsured motorist, and subsequently sought confirmation of an arbitor’s award determining his damages for the injury in Pierce County Superior Court. Sherry’s insurer, petitioner Financial Indemnity Company (FIC), objected to Sherry’s proposed judgment, claiming an entitlement to offset its under insured motorist coverage obligation by the amount of personal injury obligation it had already paid to Sherry. Both Sherry and FIC explicitly waived any objection to the trial court’s deciding the offset issue during the confirmation action. The trial court entered a judgment in favor of Sherry in which FIC was permitted to take the full personal injury protection offset, less a proportionate share of Sherry’s attorney fees. On Sherry’s appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s judgment and remanded for entry of a judgment in favor of Sherry for the full amount of the arbitration award, holding that because Sherry was not fully compensated for his damages, FIC could not take the offset. The Supreme Court of Washington granted FIC’s petition for review.
questions: Can the same trial judge who confirmed the arbitration award also resolve coverage disputes between the insured Sherry and the insurer, or should such disputes be resolved in a separate declaratory judgment action? When does an insured become “fully compensated,” allowing an insurance company to reduce judgment on an arbitration award to account for insurance benefits the insured has already received?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court concluded that since both parties orally amended their pleading to include prayer for declaratory relief, the trial court did have the authority and jurisdiction to resolve the offset dispute during the confirmation action. Also, in terms of offsetting previously paid personal injury protection benefits from underinsured motorist insurance benefits, “full compensation” does not mean the amount recoverable under underinsured motorist insurance after the reduction for the comparative amount. Instead, the insured party is fully compensated when they have made complete recovery of the actual loses suffered as a result of an automobile accident as determined by a court or arbitrator. Thus, the Court affirmed the Court of Appeals judgment that FIC has no right to an offset since Sherry had not yet been fully compensated, and the case was remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.

title: In re Personal Restraint of Borrero
facts: Petitioner Aaron Borrero was convicted of kidnapping and attempted murder in the Superior Court for King County after robbing and abducting Leslie Lemieux at gunpoint during a drug transaction and subequently attempting to drown him in the Yakima River. After exhausting his direct appeals, Borrero filed a personal restraint petition in the Supreme Court of Washington. It asserted that his convictions violated the 5th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s prohibition against double jeopardy insofar as the evidence necessary to prove the kidnapping also proved the “substantial step” element of the crime of attempted murder.
questions: Did convicting Borrero of both kidnapping and attempted murder subject him to double jeopardy?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for the Court affirmed Borrero’s convictions, concluding that although the state of Washington did not identify in its charging instrument what facts constituted the “substantial step” element of the crime of attempted murder, it is not necessary to assume that these were the same as the facts required to prove kidnapping. In particular, the Court held that as the facts establishing kidnapping are by themselves insufficient to establish attempted murder and as the facts establishing attempted murder are by themselves insufficient to establish kidnapping, Borrero was not subjected to double jeopardy.

title: State of Washington v. George
facts: Petitioners John and Tommy George were charged with attempted first degree theft by deception after accepting a cashier’s check for selling a truck over its market value to an undercover police officer. The State argued the Georges committed attempted theft by trying to steall the cashier’s check through deceiving the buyer on the value of the truck. The Georges moved for dismissal in King County Superior Court arguing the State offered no evidence showing that the truck they sold was worth less than the sale price. The Superior Court convicted the Georges, and they subsequently appealed. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction. The Supreme Court of Washington granted the Georges’ petition for review.
questions: Is “value” for the purposes of the degree of theft determined by the amount of money received or the difference between the amount and the market value of the item sold, pursuant to Wash. Rev. Code §9A.56.020?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the lower courts’ judgments, finding that the actual value of the truck was not relevant to the measure of value of the stolen property. The cashier’s check the Georges obtained was the “property of another” they intended to obtain by aid of deception, and its value exceeds $1500. In deception cases, Wash. Rev. Code §9A.56.020(1)(b) looks only at the value of the property obtained, not the net result of the exchange. Since the evidence is sufficient in finding the Georges deprived the buyer of more than $1500, the Court affirmed the convictions.

title: In re Dependency of Schermer
facts: Stephen and Margaret Schermer petitioned the Snohomish County Juvenile Court to have their son Henry declared dependent and taken into custody by the petitioner Department of Social and Health Services. The Schermers asserted that Henry’s sexually deviant behavior and other mental health problems make it unsafe for him to reside in their home and that they can no longer afford to pay for his treatment at a residential treatment facility. The juvenile court dismissed the petition, ruling that as a matter of law there is insufficient evidence to establish that Henry is dependent insofar as his parents could afford six additional months of residential treatment if they sold their home. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the case for a hearing, holding that the Schermers presented a prima facie case for dependency. The Department of Social and Health Services appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the juvenile court err in ruling as a matter of law that Henry is not dependent?
conclusions: Justice Madsen’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that a rational trier of fact could conclude that the Schermers are incapable of meeting Henry’s needs and that their inability to do so poses a substantial danger to his physical and mental health. In particular, the Court found that substantial evidence indicates that the Schermers would be unable to safely house Henry in their home. The Court also held that the Schermers’ ability to pay for residential treatment for Henry is not relevant to determing whether he is dependent and is only relevant in the context of determining the Schermers’ financial obligations after a finding of dependency.

title: Washington Citizens Action Welfare Rights Organization Coalition v. State of Washington
facts: In the 2000 general election, Initiative 722, which reduced the amount that property taxes may be increased from six percent to two percent, was passed by the voters. Litigation was immediately initiated that challenged the constitutionality of Initiative 722. While this litigation was pending, the sponsors of Initiative 747, which reduced Initiative 722’s two percent limit on property tax increases to one percent, succeeded in placing it on the ballot for the 2001 general election. However, prior to the 2001 general election, Initiative 722 was declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court of Washington in the case of Burien v. Kiga. Two months later, the voters passed Initiative 747. The respondent Washington Citizens Action Welfare Rights Organization Coalition subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a declaratory judgment that Initiative 747 is unconstitutional insofar as it does not comply with Article II §37 of the Washington State Constitution’s requirement that an initiative fully set forth the acts or sections it seeks to amend and with Article II §19 of the Washington State Constitution’s requirement that the subject of an initiative be accurately expressed in its ballot title. The superior court ruled that Initiative 747 violates Article II §37 because the invalidation of Initiative 722 rendered language in Initiative 747 indicating that it would reduce the limit on property tax increases from two percent to one percent erroneous and misleading. The state of Washington appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is Initiative 747 unconstitutionally ambiguous?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that Initiative 747 is unconstitutionally ambiguous insofar as a voter reading the text of the initiative could believe that the initiative was reducing the limit on property tax increases from two percent to one percent rather than, in actuality, from six percent to one percent. Given the substantial difference between a one percent decrease in the limit on property tax increases and a five percent decrease in the limit on property tax increases in terms of the impact upon state revenue and upon voters’ property tax burden, the Court held that Initiative 747 violates Article II §37.

title: Hegwine v. Longview Fibre Company, Inc.
facts: Petitioner Longview Fibre Company, Inc. rescinded its offer of employment to respondent Stacy Hegwine after a pre-employment medical examination revealed that she was pregnant. The stated reason for the rescission of the offer was Hegwine’s inability as a result of her pregnancy to meet the physical requirements of the position. Hegwine subsequently filed a sex discrimination claim against Longview Fibre Company. The trial court ruled in favor of Longview Fibre Company, finding that Hegwine’s pregancy was a disability that prevented her from performing essential functions of the position and that Longview Fibre Company was therefore not required to accommodate her. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that employment discrimination because of pregnancy is a form of sex discrimination governed by Washington Revised Code §49.60.180 rather than a form of disability discrimination subject to accommodation analysis. The Washington Court of Appeals also held that Longview Fibre Company’s rescission of its offer of employment to Hegwine violated §49.60.180 insofar as the physical requirements that were the stated reason for the rescission were a pretext rather than a bona fide occupational qualification. Longview Fibre Company appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is employment discrimination because of pregnancy a form of sex discrimination rather than a form of disability discrimination? If so, are the physical requirements that Longview Fibre Company stated as its reason for refusing to hire Hegwine a bona fide occupational qualification?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that although §49.60.180 does not specifically mention pregnancy, the interpretive regulations promulgated by the Washington State Human Rights Commission make it clear that employment discrimination because of pregnancy is a form of sex discrimination. The Court also found that Longview Fibre Company violated §49.60.180 when it refused to hire Hegwine as the physical requirements that it stated as its reason for rescinding its offer were a pretext rather than a bona fide occupational qualification. The Court based this conclusion upon the fact that Longview Fibre Company made no mention of these requirements until after it discovered that Hegwine was pregnant and the fact that it offered no evidence that substantially all pregnant women are incapable of performing the essential functions of the position.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Day
facts: Following petitioner Jeffrey Day’s conviction for child molestation, the respondent Washington State Bar Association commenced disciplinary proceedings against him. Day was subsequently disbarred after a hearing. Day appealed the disciplinary board’s sanction to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that it should have applied the American Bar Association standards’ presumptive sanction of suspension for criminal conduct that adversely reflects on an attorney’s fitness to practice, that it failed to consider mitigating factors, and that the sanction is disproportionate in light of the sanctions imposed in similar cases.
questions: Did the disciplinary board err in failing to apply the American Bar Association standards’ presumptive sanction of suspension? Did the disciplinary board fail to consider mitigating factors? Is the sanction of disbarment disproportionate in light of the sanctions imposed in similar cases?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed Day’s disbarment, concluding that the disciplinary board did not err in deviating from the American Bar Association standards’ presumptive sanction of suspension insofar as the victim of Day’s molestation was a former client whose trust was violated. The Court also held that while the disciplinary board did not err in failing to consider Day’s criminal sentence and his cooperative attitude toward the proceedings as mitigating factors, it did err in failing to consider Day’s selfish motive as an aggravating factor. Finally, the Court found that disbarment is a proportionate sanction despite the fact that other cases involving sexual misconduct have resulted in suspensions as these cases are distinguishable given that they involved consensual sex and did not involve minors.

title: In re Detention of Elmore
facts: Pursuant to Washington Revised Code §71.09, petitioner Keith Elmore petitioned the Superior Court for Clark County for a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released from his civil commitment as a sexually violent predator. The superior court granted the petition, ruling that Elmore presented a prima facie case for release. The state of Washington appealed, asserting that the 2005 amendments to §71.09, which stipulate that a sexually violent predator’s advance in age is by itself insufficient to establish probable cause for a trial, apply retroactively to Elmore and that Elmore therefore failed to present a prima facie case for release. The Washington Court of Appeals reversed the superior court, holding that Elmore is not entitled to a trial. Elmore appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the 2005 amendments to §71.09 apply retroactively to Elmore? If not, did Elmore present a prima facie case for release?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the legislature did not intend for the 2005 amendments to §71.09 to apply retroactively. Thus, the Court held that Elmore’s advance in age, coupled with the other evidence presented by Elmore of changes in his condition in response to treatment, established probable cause for a trial to decide whether he should be unconditionally released.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Qwest Corporation v. Bellevue
facts: Respondent Qwest Corporation petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a declaratory judgment that the petitioner city of Bellevue may not lawfully assess a utility occupation tax on charges for access to interstate telecommunication services or on other federally tariffed charges. The superior court granted summary judgment for Qwest Company. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the question of whether a charge is a charge for access to interstate or intrastate telecommunication services a question of fact or a question of law? Are all federally tariffed charges charges for access to interstate telecommunication services?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that the question of whether a charge is a charge for access to interstate or intrastate telecommunication services is a question of law that is not determined by customers’ actual use of the connections. The Court also held that any federally tarifed charges are charges for access to interstate telecommunication services. Thus, as Washington Revised Code §35A.82.060(1) prohibits cities from taxing revenue derived from charges for access to interstate telecommunication services, the Court found that the superior court had properly granted summary judgment for Qwest Corporation.

title: Hornback v. Wentworth
questions: Whether a real estate contract should have been rescinded under RCW 58.17.210.

title: State of Washington v. Chamberlin
facts: Petitioner Scott Chamberlin was convicted of possession of methamphetamine with intent to deliver in the Superior Court for Island County after a search of his home occasioned by information provided by an informant revealed methamphetamine. Chamberlin appealed his conviction directly to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that the judge who presided over the suppression hearing should have recused himself as he was the same judge who had issued the search warrant for Chamberlin’s home. Chamberlin also asserted that the search warrant lacked probable cause.
questions: Should a judge automatically recuse themself from hearing a challenge to a search warrant that they themself issued? Did probable cause exist to search Chamberlin’s home?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed Chamberlin’s conviction, concluding that no inherent bias or prejudice results from a judge that issued a search warrant presiding over a subsequent suppression hearing in which the validity of the warrant is challenged. The Court also held that probable cause existed to search Chamberlin’s home insofar as the informant made statements against their penal interest and provided detailed information regarding drug transactions that he engaged in with Chamberlin.

title: In re Jack Lee Burtch, Attorney at Law
questions: Show cause hearing.

title: Stevens v. Brink's Home Security, Inc.
facts: Respondent David Stevens and other technicians employed by petitioner Brink’s Home Security, Inc. filed a class action suit against Brink’s Home Security in the Superior Court for King County. The technicians alleged that Brink’s Home Security violated the Minimum Wage Act (Washington Revised Code §49.46) when it refused to compensate them for time spent driving company cars between their homes and their first and last jobsites of the workday. The trial court granted summary judgment for Stevens and awarded Stevens and the other technicians back pay with interest and attorney’s fees. Brink’s Home Security appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Brink’s Home Security violate §49.46 when it refused to compensate its technicians for time spent driving company cars between their homes and their first and last jobsites of the workday? If so, did the trial court err in awarding the technicians prejudgment interest and attorney’s fees?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that the technicians are on duty during the time that they spend driving company cars between their homes and their first and last jobsites of the workday and that Brink’s Home Security’s refusal to compensate them for this time violates §49.46. In particular, the Court held that the company cars constitute workplaces insofar as the technicians’ use of these cars is strictly controlled by Brink’s Home Security, with the technicians prohibited from using the cars for personal business and required to be available to assist at other jobsites while using them, even while en route to and from their homes. The Court also held that the trial court properly awarded the technicians prejudgment interest given that their damages are liquidated damages that can be determined with exactness. Finally, the Court found that the technicians are also entitled to attorney’s fees.

title: Herring v. Todd Shipyards Corporation
facts: Respondent Roger Herring filed suit against petitioner Todd Shipyards Corporation after being diagnosed with mesothelioma caused by his exposure to asbestos while working for subcontractors of Todd Shipyards. Todd Shipyards successfully moved for summary judgment, arguing that Herring’s claim had been discharged when it filed for bankruptcy seventeen years earlier. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Todd Shipyards should have given notice of its bankruptcy to Herring’s union as it was reasonably ascertainable to Todd Shipyards that it would be liable to union members for asbestos-related claims. Todd Shipyards appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Herring entitled to actual notice of Todd Shipyards’ bankruptcy?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that as Herring was not a known creditor, he was not entitled to actual notice of Todd Shipyards’ bankruptcy but rather was merely entitled to the publication notice that Todd Shipyards provided. Thus, although it was reasonably ascertainable to Todd Shipyards that it would be liable to members of Herring’s union for asbestos-related claims, the Court held that debtors are not required to provide actual notice to everyone who could potentially have been affected by their actions.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Perez-Pena
facts: Petitioner Fernando Perez-Pena was charged with assaulting a client during the course of representation and failing to return unearned legal fees by the Washington State Bar Association’s Disciplinary Board, in violation of Washington Rules of Profession Conduct 8.4(i) and 1.15(d) respectively. Before the commencement of the disciplinary proceedings, Perez-Pena was convicted of misdemeanor assault and the client obtained a civil judgment against Perez-Pena in the amount of the unearned fee. The court later vacated the judgment and sentence and dismissed the complaint, but did not vacate the jury’s conviction. After weighing the mitigating and aggravating factors the disciplinary hearing officer found the evidence supported the charge of assaulting the client, but did not support the charge of failing to return unearned legal fees, and recommended admonishment. The Disciplinary Board unanimously amended the hearing officer’s sanction for the first charge to a three-month suspension, and reversed the finding on the second charge leading to a concurrent six-month suspension, along with making Perez-Pena’s reinstatement be conditioned on restitution of the unearned fee. Perez-Pena appealed to the Supreme Court of Washington to review the severity of the sanction. He argued Wash. Rev. Code §9.96.030 released him of all penalties from the offense because his conviction was vacated, and the hearing officer improperly relied on his assault conviction as conclusive evidence he committed the act.
questions: Does dismissal of the complaint and vacation of the judgment and sentence constitute a vacation of a person’s conviction? If it does not, did the hearing officer improperly rely on the assault conviction as conclusive evidence of Perez-Pena’s guilt? Did the Disciplinary Board arrive at an appropriate sanction after weighing the mitigating and aggravating factors?
conclusions: Justice Bobbe J. Bridge wrote the opinion for the Court concluding the hearing officer did not improperly rely on Perez-Pena’s assault conviction as conclusive evidence he committed the act, because Perez-Pena did not appropriately vacate the conviction in the manner prescribed by Wash. Rev. Code §9.96.030(1), which states the guilty verdict must also be set aside to constitute the vacation of a person’s conviction. In reviewing the discrepancy between the hearing officer and Disciplinary Board’s weighing of the mitigating and aggravating factors, the Court found the hearing officer’s sanction was too lenient, while also finding the Disciplinary Board was incorrect in finding additional mitigating factors leading to the harsher sanction. Thus, the Court imposed a 60-day suspension along with the condition of Perez-Pena’s reinstatement depending upon satisfaction of returning the unearned fee.

title: Erwin v. Cotter Health Care Ctrs., Inc.
facts: Respondent Cary Erwin filed suit against petitioners James F. Cotter and Cotter Health Centers Inc. in Yakima County Superior Court to collect commissions and fees arising from Cotter’s leasing of several senior health care facilities in California and Texas. According to the dispute selection clause of their contractual agreement, any disputes would be resolved under Washington law and in Washington courts. Cotter argued the contractual choice of Washington law is ineffective, and that California law should govern the dispute. Cotter also argues that under California law Erwin is prohibited from claiming leasing fees since he is not a licensed real estate broker in the state, whereas Erwin argues that under Washington Law, specifically Wash. Rev. Code §18.85, he is allowed to claim leasing fees for work done outside of Washington. The trial court ruled in favor Erwin, holding the contractual choice of choosing Washington jurisdiction for disputes is effective, entitling Erwin to the leasing fees. Cotter appealed, declaring Erwin did not act as a real estate broker when working outside of Washington. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court’s judgment, while recognizing that under California law Erwin’s work was not considered that of a “real estate broker.” The Supreme Court of Washington granted Cotter’s petition for review.
questions: Did Erwin act as a “real estate broker” in providing services to cotter under their contractual agreements? Is the parties’ contractual choice of Washington Law effective? Under the applicable law, can Erwin, a Washington-licensed real estate broker, maintain a claim for fees arising from the leasing of Cotter’s California senior health care facilities?
conclusions: Justice Mary E. Fairhurst wrote the opinion for a unanimous court concluding that Erwin did act as a real estate broker when applying the definitions from either Washington law or California law to the language in their contractual agreement, thus reversing the Court of Appeals in part. Affirming the judgment of Court of Appeals and trial court, the Court concluded that the parties’ contractual choice-of-law provision placing all disputes under the jurisdiction of Washington law is effective. Finally, since Washington law does govern the dispute, pursuant to Wash. Rev. Code §18.85 Erwin can maintain a claim for the fees arising from the leasing of Cotter’s California facilities. The Court remanded the case to the trial court for actions consistent with this opinion.

title: Beal Bank, S.S.B. v. Sarich
facts: Respondent Steven Sarich and his wife Kay took out a loan with Washington Mutual Bank secured with a deed of trust on their home. Sarich subsequently took out two additional loans with U.S. Bank that used the same home as security. After Sarich defaulted, Washington Mutual Bank, as the senior lienholder, foreclosed on the home, which was sold at a trustee’s sale. Following the sale, petitioner Beal Bank, S.S.B., to which U.S. Bank had assigned both loans, petitioned the Superior Court for King County for a judgment against Sarich for the amount of both outstanding loans. The superior court granted summary judgment for Sarich, ruling that, under Washington Revised Code §61.24.100, the foreclosure of a senior lienholder’s deed of trust precludes an action by a junior lienholder to recover on a debt secured by a deed of trust on the same property. Beal Bank appealed the superior court’s decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does §61.24.100 preclude an action by a junior lienholder to recover on a debt secured by a deed of trust following the foreclosure of a senior lienholder’s deed of trust on the same property?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the superior court and remanded the case, concluding that although Beal Bank’s rights in the collateral were extinguished by the foreclosure and sale of Sarich’s home, the underlying debt was not extinguished as §61.24.100 does not implicate the rights of junior lienholders.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Densley v. Department of Retirement Systems
facts: Petitioner James Densley, a retired Pierce County prosecuting attorney enrolled in the Washington Public Employee Retirement System, requested retirement service credit for summer training exercises and weekend drills he participated in as a member of the Washington Army National Guard. The respondent Department of Retirement Systems denied Densley’s request, ruling that Washington Revised Code §41.40.170(3), which grants public employees retirement service credit for military service, applies only to active military service. Densley subsequently petitioned the Superior Court for Pierce County for review. The superior court affirmed the Department of Retirement Systems’ decision. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is §41.40.170(3)’s grant of retirement service credit for military service limited to active military service? If not, is Densley entitled to retirement service credit for his participation in summer training exercises and weekend drills as a member of the Washington Army National Guard? Is Densley entitled to retirement service credit for his time spent traveling to and from active duty?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for the Court reversed the superior court, concluding that §41.40.170(3) grants retirement service credit for all military service and is not limited to active military service. The Court held that Densley is therefore entitled to retirement service credit for his participation in summer training exercises as a member of the Washington Army National Guard. However, the Court also held that Densley is not entitled to retirement service credit for his participation in weekend drills as the statute governing retirement service credit in effect at the time of Densley’s service (former Washington Revised Code §41.40.010(9)) only granted retirement service credit when ten or more days were worked in a given calendar month. Finally, the Court found that Densley is entitled to retirement service credit for his time spent traveling to and from active duty as such travel is considered part of active duty by the federal government and federal courts.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Tobin
facts: Petitioner Douglas Tobin was convicted of illegally harvesting crab and geoduck in the Superior Court for Pierce County and was ordered to pay $1,735,596 in restitution to the state of Washington. Tobin appealed the restitution order, asserting that the environmental, investigative, and administrative costs included in the restitution award were insufficiently related to his crimes. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the restitution order. Tobin appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: May environmental, investigative, and administrative costs be included in a restitution award under Washington Revised Code §9.94A.753?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for the Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that environmental costs that capture the real ecological value of the damage inflicted by the predicate crime may be included in restitution awards under §9.94A.753 so long as they are sufficiently causally related to the predicate crime. The Court also held that restitution awards may also include public costs such as investigative and administrative costs.

title: In re post-sentence review of Leach
facts: Respondent Yulanda Leach pleaded guilty to attempted assault of a child in the second degree, and was sentenced to 23.25 months confinement and between nine and 18 months community custody. The Department of Corrections petitioned for post-sentence review on the community custody component of the sentence, arguing “attempted assault” of a child is not a specifically enumerated offense for which a defendant can be sentenced to community custody according to Wash. Rev. Code §9.94A.715. The Washington Court of Appeals denied the Department of Correction’s petition, holding that attempted second degree assault of a child qualifies for a term of community custody and that the conviction can be included in the illustrative examples of “crimes against persons” found under Wash. Rev. Code §9.94A.411(2). The Supreme Court of Washington granted the Department of Corrections’ petition for review.
questions: Can a court sentence an offender to community custody for attempted second degree assault of a child, even though “attempted Assault” is not on the enumerated list of offenses described as “crimes against persons?” Should the list be viewed as illustrative examples, or as an exclusive and complete designation of crimes sufficient for community custody sentencing?
conclusions: Justice Richard B. Sanders’ opinion for the Court concluded that the Department of Corrections was correct in arguing a court cannot add “attempted assault” or any other anticipatory offenses to Wash. Rev. Code 9.94A.411(2) as judicial gloss because the statute presents an exhausted list of “crimes against persons.” Nothing in the statute suggests the list should be viewed as illustrative, and the legislature plainly meant for the 47 enumerated crimes to be the exclusive and complete list of “crimes against persons,” which does not include “attempted assault.” The Court remanded the case to the trial court for resentencing without community custody.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Indoor Billboard, Inc. v. Integra Telecom of Washington, Inc.
facts: Asserting violations of the Consumer Protection Act (Washington Revised Code §19.86), petitioner Indoor Billboard, Inc. filed suit against respondent Integra Telecom of Washington, Inc. in the Superior Court for King County. Indoor Billboard alleged that Integra Telecom engaged in an unfair or deceptive practice by charging its Washington local service customers a surcharge that it falsely labeled as a presubscribed interexchange carrier charge (a type of surcharge permitted under Federal Communications Commission regulations). The superior court granted summary judgment for Integra Telecom, ruling that Indoor Billboard failed as a matter of law to establish that Integra Telecom engaged in an unfair or deceptive practice and that the voluntary payment doctrine bars Indoor Billboard’s claim in any event. Indoor Billboard appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the superior court have subject matter jurisdiction to decide Indoor Billboard’s Consumer Protection Act claim? If so, did the superior court err in ruling that Indoor Billboard failed as a matter of law to establish that Integra Telecom engaged in an unfair or deceptive practice? Does the voluntary payment doctrine bar Indoor Billboard’s claim?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the superior court. The Court concluded that the superior court had subject matter jurisdiction to decide Indoor Billboard’s Consumer Protection Act claim insofar as the claim was not one for services not received, in which case the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission would have subject matter jurisdiction, but rather a claim of an unfair or deceptive practice brought pursuant to §19.86. The Court also held that Integra Telecom engaged in an unfair or deceptive practice as a matter of law insofar as its labeling of the surcharge had the potential to deceive a substantial portion of its customers into thinking that the surcharge was authorized by the Federal Communications Commission. Finally, the Court found that the voluntary payment doctrine has no place as an affirmative defense in the Consumer Protection Act Context. Thus, the Court remanded the case to the superior court for trial.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Morin v. Harrell
facts: Petitioner Melanie Morin brought suit against respondent employer Clarence Harrell for unpaid overtime wages. Harrell challenged the constitutionality of Initiative 518 enacted in 1988 that amended the Minimum Wage Act, Wash. Rev. Code §49.46, by replacing the exemption for domestic service providers with an exemption limited to individuals employed in casual labor. The Superior Court of Kittias County granted summary judgment in favor of the respondent, holding I-518 violated Art. II, Sect. 19 of the Washington State Constitution that requires the subject of a bill be expressed in its title. Morin’s motion for reconsideration was denied, she appealed to the Washington Court of Appeals, and the case was transferred to the Supreme Court of Washington for direct review.
questions: Did the trial court err in granting summary judgment to the respondent as a matter of law based on the alleged unconstitutionality of I-518?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court held that the subsequent amendments to Wash. Rev. Code §4.96.010 in 1989 cured any alleged defect in the title of I-518 because the court previously established that any later amendment to or reenactment of a statute supersedes and therefore “cure[s] any defect” in the earlier legislation. Wash. Rev. Code §4.96.010 was amended to eliminated the exception to the Minimum Wage Act for domestic service providers pursuant to I-518. Thus, the Court reversed the trial court’s summary judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Beaupre v. Pierce County
facts: Respondent Curtis Beaupre, an officer with the Pierce County Sheriff’s Office, filed suit against petitioner Pierce County in the Superior Court for King County after he was accidentally injured by another officer while pursuing a suspect. Pierce County moved for summary judgment, asserting that the professional rescue doctrine bars Beaupre’s suit. The superior court denied the motion for summary judgment, ruling that the professional rescue doctrine does not apply. Pierce County appealed this ruling to the Washington Court of Appeals, which transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the professional rescue doctrine bar Beaupre from recovering damages for injuries suffered in the line of duty as a result of the negligence of another officer?
conclusions: Justice Owens’ opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that while the professional rescue doctrine bars professional rescuers such as police officers from recovering damages for injuries suffered as a result of the hazards inherent to a particular rescue activity, it does not bar professional rescuers from recovering damages for injuries suffered as a result of independent or intervening hazards not reasonably foreseen. Thus, as the negligence of Beaupre’s fellow officer was an intervening hazard not reasonably foreseen, the Court held that the professional rescue doctrine does not bar Beaupre’s suit.

title: State of Washington v. Foxhoven
facts: Petitioner Lawrence Foxhoven was convicted of malicious mischief in the Superior Court for Whatcom County after etching graffiti on the windows of several businesses. Foxhoven appealed his conviction, asserting that the trial court’s admission of evidence of his prior criminal history of graffiti violated Washington Rule of Evidence 404(b), which excludes evidence of prior bad acts when that evidence is used for the purpose of proving conformity with those acts on a different occasion. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Foxhoven’s conviction. Foxhoven appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the trial court’s admission of evidence of Foxhoven’s prior criminal history of graffiti violate Washington Rule of Evidence 404(b)’s exclusion of evidence of prior bad acts?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that evidence of Foxhoven’s prior criminal history of graffiti had been properly admitted to show identity insofar as the tags used in both instances of graffiti were identical.

title: King v. King
facts: After petitioner Brenda King and respondent Michael King filed for divorce, Michael King moved to be named the primary residential parent for their three children. At the subsequent custody hearing, Michael King was represented by counsel while Brenda King appeared pro se due to her indigency. The trial court awarded Michael King primary residential care of the children and decision-making authority. Brenda King subsequently moved for a new hearing and requested that counsel be appointed at public expense to represent her. The trial court denied the motion, ruling that it lacked authority to appoint counsel to represent Brenda King insofar as the legislature has not authorized funding for representation for indigent parties in child custody hearings. Brenda King appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does an indigent party in a child custody hearing have a constitutional right to representation at public expense?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that no right to representation at public expense exists in a child custody hearing. In particular, the Court held that no such right exists insofar as child custody hearings are private actions to which the state is not a party and the full resources of the state are not brought to bear. Moreover, while a parent’s interest in the provisions of parenting plan is significant, fundamental parental liberty interests are not at stake as such plans do not terminate the parental rights of either parent. Thus, the Court found that while indigent parents have a constitutional right to representation at public expense in termination and dependency proceedings, this right does not extend to child custody hearings.

title: Delaney v. The Board of Spokane County Commissioners
questions: Must the Board of Spokane County Commissioners establish and fund a tenth district court judge position?

title: Ludvigsen v. Seattle
facts: Petitioner Mark Ludvigsen was charged with driving under the influence of alcohol in 2002 after submitting to a breath test. When Ludvigsen went to trial in 2005, the law governing the validity of breath tests had changed. In particular, under the 2004 amendments to Seattle Municipal Code §11.56.020(A)(1)(a), the city no obligates itself to demonstrate that the test thermometer is certified. Thus, while the results of Ludvigsen’s breath test would have inadmissible under §11.56.020(A)(1)(a) prior to 2004, they were admissible under the amended version of §11.56.020(A)(1)(a). The trial court ruled that the amendments do not apply retroactively. The city of Seattle appealed this ruling to the Superior Court for King County, which reversed, holding that the amendments are procedural in nature and therefore are assumed to apply retroactively. Ludvigsen appealed this decision to the Washington Court of Appeals, which certified the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Do the amendments to §11.56.020(A)(1)(a) regarding the validity of breath tests apply retroactively?
conclusions: Justice Chambers’ opinion for the Court reversed the superior court, concluding that the amendments to §11.56.020(A)(1)(a) were not merely procedural in nature insofar as they changed the quantum of evidence necessary to support a conviction. In particular, prior to the amendments, defendants could not be prosecuted as a matter of law solely on the basis of the results of an uncertified breath test. Thus, the Court held that to apply the amendments retroactively to Ludvigsen’s case, which would therefore otherwise be dismissed, would violate Article I §10 of the United States Constitution’s prohibition against ex post facto laws.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Reep
facts: After responding to a fire at the home of petitioner David Reep’s parents that was apparently the result of the methamphetamine manufacturing process, police officers obtained a warrant to search Reep’s bedroom for methamphetamine-related items. While executing the warrant, the officers found photographs stored on Reep’s computer that they considered suspicious and obtained another warrant to search for items related to “child sex.” This search revealed photographs taken of children without their knowledge that Reep subsequently admitted were taken for the purpose of arousing or gratifying his sexual desire. Consequently, Reep was convicted of four counts of voyeurism. Reep appealed his conviction, asserting that the search warrant violated the 4th Amendment to the United States Constitution’s requirement of particularity and that the evidence derived from it should therefore have been suppressed. The Washington Court of Appeals transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the term “child sex” describe with sufficient particularity the items to be seized?
conclusions: Justice Sanders’ opinion for the Court reversed Reep’s conviction and remanded the case, concluding that the term “child sex” did not describe with sufficient particularity the items to be seized insofar as it is broad and ambiguous and encompasses constitutionally protected material.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Feature Realty, Inc. v. Preston Gates Ellis, L.L.P.
facts: Petitioner Feature Realty, Inc. filed a malpractice claim against Terrence Butler and Jerry Neal, its former attorneys, and the law firm of Preston Gates Ellis, L.L.P. in the Superior Court for Los Angeles County, California. Preston Gates Ellis moved to stay the case indefinitely on grounds of forum non conveniens and Neal moved to quash the service of process for lack of personal jurisdiction. The superior court granted both motions and issued a six month continuation to allow Feature Realty to refile the action in Washington. Feature Realty subsequently refiled the action in the Superior Court for King County and filed a request for dismissal with the Superior Court for Los Angeles County. However, having failed to timely serve the defendants with the complaint filed in the Superior Court for King County, Feature Realty voluntarily dismissed the case shortly thereafter. When Feature Realty refiled the case with new counsel, the defendants moved for summary judgment, asserting that the second dismissal of the case constituted an adjudication on the merits under Washington State Court Rule 41, which bars cases that have twice been voluntarily and unilaterally dismissed from being refiled. The trial court granted the motion and dismissed the case. Feature Realty appealed the trial court’s decision, arguing that the first dismissal was neither voluntary nor unilateral insofar as it was compelled by the Superior Court for Los Angeles County’s indefinite staying of the case against Preston Gates Ellis on grounds of forum non conveniens and its ruling that it lacked personal jurisdiction over Neal. The Washington Court of Appeals transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Was Feature Realty’s first request for dismissal voluntary and unilateral?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the trial court, concluding that Washington State Court Rule 41’s bar against refiling a case after a second voluntary and unilateral dismissal is non-discretionary and applies regardless of the plaintiff’s intent in seeking dismissal. Thus, as Feature Realty later obtained a second dismissal, the case could not be refiled.

title: Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company v. Martinelli
facts: Petitioners Joseph and Karen Martinelli initiated arbitration proceedings against Dan Paulson Construction, Inc., alleging that Dan Paulson Construction and its subcontractors performed defective work in constructing their home. Dan Paulson Construction subsequently tendered defense in the arbitration proceeding to its insurer, respondent Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company. Prior to the arbitration hearing, Dan Paulson Construction and the Martinellis agreed that any award would be a lump sum award. Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company responded by petitioning the Superior Court for San Juan County for a declaratory judgment as to which of the Martinellis’ claims are covered under Dan Paulson Construction’s insurance policy and, consequently, what portion of any lump sum award would be payable by Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company. Pursuant to this declaratory judgment action, Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company issued a subpoena to the arbitrator. After the Martinellis protested Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company’s ex parte communication with the arbitrator, Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company dismissed its declaratory judgment action. However, when the Martinellis reached a settlement with Dan Paulson Construction, Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company filed another declaratory judgment action in the Superior Court for San Juan County in an effort to determine what portion of the settlement amount is attributable to claims covered under Dan Paulson Construction’s insurance policy. The Martinellis counterclaimed that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company breached the duty it owed to Dan Paulson Construction and acted in bad faith. The superior court granted summary judgment for the Martinellis. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company had not acted in bad faith insofar as it had a reasonable need to know the elements of a potential award. The Martinellis appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company act in bad faith when it initiated ex parte communication with the arbitrator? If so, did Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company successfully rebut the presumption of harm arising from its bad faith conduct? Did Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company raise a genuine issue of material fact regarding the reasonableness of the settlement?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company acted in bad faith when it initiated ex parte communication with the arbitrator insofar as this contact directly interfered with the defense it was providing Dan Paulson Construction and insofar as it was not necessitated by a reasonable need to know the elements of a potential award given that it would not have been automatically liable to pay the entire settlement amount. The Court also held that Mutual of Enumclaw Insurance Company did not successfully rebut the presumption of harm arising from its bad faith conduct as this conduct interfered with Dan Paulson Construction’s hearing preparation, interjected insurance coverage issues into the arbitration, and created uncertainty regarding the potential prejudicing of the arbitrator and the confirmability of the award. Finally, the Court found that no genuine issue of material fact exists regarding the reasonableness of the settlement.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: State of Washington v. Williams
facts: Petitioner Demetrius Williams was charged with the possession of a controlled substance and released on bail. When Williams subsequently failed to appear at an omnibus hearing, he was also charged with and later convicted of bail jumping. Williams appealed his conviction, asserting that the document charging him with bail jumping based on the underlying charge of possession of a controlled substance was insufficient insofar as it failed to identify the penalty class of the charge for which he failed to appear. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Williams’ conviction. Williams appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did its failure to include the penalty class of the underlying charge render the charging document insufficient?
conclusions: Justice James M. Johnson’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the charging document was sufficient as the penalty class of the underlying charge is not one of the elements of the crime of bail jumping under Washington Revised Code §9A.76.170. Thus, although the penalty for bail jumping is determined by the penalty class of the underlying charge, it need not be included in the charging document or in the instructions to the jury.

title: State of Washington v. Varnell
facts: Petitioner Mitchell Varnell was convicted of four counts of solicitation to commit murder in the Superior Court for Snohomish County after offering an undercover police officer $60,000 to murder his ex-wife, her brother, and both of her parents. Varnell appealed his convictions, asserting that his solicitation of the murder of four people in a single conversation constitutes a single unit of prosecution of solicitation to commit murder. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Varnell’s convictions. Varnell appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Varnell’s solicitation of the murder of four people in a single conversation constitute one unit of prosecution or four under Washington Revised Code §9A.28.030?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and reversed three of Varnell’s four convictions, concluding that §9A.28.030’s unit of prosecution is the number of solicitations rather than the number of objects of the solicitation.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Atchison v. Great Western Malting Company
facts: Petitioner Kaela Atchison, the personal representative of her deceased father William Atchison’s estate, filed a wrongful death action against his former employer, respondent Great Western Malting Company, in the Superior Court for Clark County, claiming that workplace exposure to pesticides and contaminated dust was the cause of the cancer that led to his death. The superior court dismissed the action on grounds that the three year statute of limitations had expired. Atchison appealed the superior court’s decision, asserting that as she was a minor at the time of her father’s death and therefore ineligible to be appointed personal respresentative of his estate and to bring a wrongful death action, the statute of limitations tolled until she reached her majority. The Washington Court of Appeals transferred the case to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the statute of limitations toll during the period between William Atchison’s death and Kaela Atchison reaching her majority?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that the relevant tolling statute (Washington Revised Code §4.20.020) becomes operative only when the personal representative of the decedent’s estate is disabled and is not tolled by the minority of a beneficiary of the decedent’s assets. Thus, as Kaela Atchison did not become the personal representative of her deceased father’s estate until after she reached her majority, the statute of limitations did not toll.

title: Locke v. Seattle
facts: Respondents Kevin Locke and personal representative of Gary Lindell brought suit against petitioner city of Seattle for injuries sustained during Locke’s employment as a fire fighter trainee, and Lindell’s wrongful death in a police officer training exercise. In both cases, the city challenged the “right to sue” provision in the Washington Law Enforcement Officers’ and Fire Fighters’ Retirement System Act (Washington Revised Code §41.26.281), arguing that it violates the city’s sovereign immunity and the privileges and immunities clause of Article I §12 of the Washington State Constitution. The Superior Court for King County ruled in favor Locke and Lindell’s personal representative, holding the city liable for the injuries and wrongful death sustained during their employment. The city appealed in both cases, in which the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court ruling in Locke, holding the statute granting municipal employees the right to take action is not unconstitutional, and denied review of the Lindell case referring to the opinion laid down in Locke. The cases were consolidated upon review by the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does the LEOFF “right to sue” provision violate the city’s sovereign immunity? Likewise, does the LEOFF “right to sue” provision violate the privileges and immunities clause of the Washington State Constitution?
conclusions: Justice Owens' opinion for a unanimous Court held that the statute granting a municipal employee a “right to sue” abrogates the City’s sovereign immunity according to Wash. Rev. Code §4.96.010. Furthermore, since the city is a considered a municipal corporation, it does not have standing to bring a privileges and immunities claim. Thus, the Court affirmed the Court of Appeals judgment and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: State of Washington v. Hatchie
facts: Petitioner Raymond Hatchie was convicted of unlawful manufacture of a controlled substance after being denied a motion to suppress the evidence of methamphetamine manufacturing equipment seen by police in his home when they were looking for a suspect pursuant to an arrest warrant. Hatchie argued a misdemeanor arrest warrant does not give police the “authority of law” to enter a private residence, and that the police had no probable cause to believe the suspect was a resident at Hatchie’s home. Hatchie also claimed he was not given a chance to allocate until after the trial judge orally announced his proposed sentence. The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed the conviction, and the Supreme Court of Washington granted Hatchie’s petition for review.
questions: Does a misdemeanor arrest warrant provide police with the “authority of law” to enter a private residence? Did the trial court violate Hatchie’s right to allocution before sentencing?
conclusions: Justice Richard Sanders’ opinion for the Court held that an arrest warrant- even for a misdemeanor- constitutes “authority of law” which allows the police the limited power to enter a residence for an arrest, as long as the entry is reasonable, the entry is not a pretext for conducting other authorized searches or investigations, the police have probable cause to believe the person named in the arrest warrant is an actual resident of the home and is present at the time of entry. The police thus had probable cause to believe the house was the suspect’s, and their entry and plain view observation of Hatchie’s methamphetamine manufacturing equipment was under authority of law. The Court also held that Hatchie failed to preserve any possible violation of his right to allocution because his defense counsel failed to properly object at trial to the judge’s giving an oral sentence before allowing Hatchie a chance to speak. The Court affirmed the Court of Appeals’ judgment.

title: J&J Celcom v. AT&T Wireless Services, Inc.
facts: J&J Celcom acquired fractional interests in several regional cellular telephone partnerships in which AT&T Wireless Services, Inc. was the majority partner. AT&T Wireless Services subsequently invoked its majority interest and voted to buy out J&J Celcom, offering to buy out J&J Celcom at a price higher than a third party appraisal. After J&J Celcom declined this offer, AT&T Wireless Services voted to sell the assets of the partnerships at their appraised value to an affiliated party, dissolve the partnerships, and pay J&J Celcom its prorated share of the sale proceeds. J&J Celcom responded by filing suit against AT&T Wireless Services in the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington, alleging that AT&T Wireless Services’ actions breached its duty of loyalty to the partnership and to its partner. The district court granted summary judgment for AT&T Wireless Services. Upon appeal, the United States Circuit Court for the Ninth Circuit certified to the Supreme Court of Washington the question of whether, under Washington’s Revised Uniform Partnership Act (Washington Revised Code §25.05.165), a controlling partner who causes the partnership to sell its assets to an affiliated party violates their duty of loyalty.
questions: Does a controlling partner who causes the partnership to sell its assets to an affiliated party violate their duty of loyalty?
conclusions: Justice Charles W. Johnson’s opinion for the Court concluded that a controlling partner who causes the partnership to sell its assets to an affiliated party does not violate their duty of loyalty under §25.05.165 In particular, the Court held that as the partnership agreement did not preclude the sale of assets and as the price paid was fair, no breach of duty occurred.

title: City of Seattle v. Klein & Deibert
