facts: Petitioner City of Seattle filed a motion to dismiss respondents Stephen Klein’s and Melissa Deibert’s right to appeal their underlying conviction in light of subsequent arrest warrants issued as a result of failing to appear at their respective review hearings after appealing their convictions. Klein and Deibert argued their appeals cannot be dismissed because they had not made a voluntary, knowing, and intelligent waiver of their constitutional right to appeal. The City claimed the Fugitive Disentitlement Doctrine (FDD) serves to abrogate the respondents’ constitutionally guaranteed right to appeal. The King County Superior Court agreed with Klein and Deibert and denied the City’s motion in both cases. The City’s petition for discretionary review was granted by the Division One Court of Appeals, and the cases were consolidated for transfer to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Does Klein's and Diebert’s failure to appear at their review hearings present the appropriate circumstances to substitute involuntary forfeiture for the required knowing waiver of the right to appeal?
conclusions: Justice James Johnson’s opinion for the Court held that the FDD could not deprive someone of his or her constitutionally guaranteed right to appeal, even if it is applied after the appeal had been filed. Even though Klein and Deibert admit they failed to appear at their review hearings, this is not evidence that they had made a voluntary, knowing, and intelligent waiver of their right to appeal their convictions. Affirming the trial court’s judgment, the Court concluded that dismissing Klein’s and Deibert’s appeals based strictly on their absence from a review hearing would violate their constitutional right to appeal.

title: Preview Properties, Inc. v. Landis
facts: Respondent Preview Properties Inc. initiated an interpleader action in the Superior Court for King County to settle the demands to earnest money from an expired real estate purchase and sale agreement between petitioner seller Brad Landis and buyer Layne Sapp, who was represented by the respondent. Landis filed a cross complaint against Sapp for the earnest money and a counter-claim against Preview, alleging statutory and common law conversion, violation of the Consumer Protection Act, and violations of real estate licensing fiduciary and statutory duties under Wash. Rev. Code §18.86.030. After Landis and Sapp stipulated Landis was entitled to the earnest money, the trial court dismissed the cross-claim against Sapp and granted summary judgment in favor of Landis in his claims against Preview, awarding damages and attorney fees. Upon Preview’s appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed the trial court’s entire judgment in favor of Landis, but did not address the judgment for Landis on his claim for Preview’s breach of statutory real estate broker licensee duties. The Supreme Court of Washington granted Landis’ appeal to review the Court of Appeals’ reversal of the entire judgment.
questions: Did the Court of Appeals err by reversing the trial court’s entire judgment, since it did not address the judgment for Landis on the issue of Preview’s violation of common law fiduciary duties and Wash. Rev. Code §18.86.030 real estate broker licensee duties?
conclusions: The Court held per curiam that the Court of Appeals erred by reversing the trial court’s entire judgment because the opinion only addresses the trial court’s ruling on Landis’ Consumer Protection and common law conversion claims, resulting in a favorable ruling of Preview’s characterization of the issues. However, since Preview did not challenge the trial court’s findings which indicated that Preview knowingly misrepresented to Landis that Sapp had signed two extensions of the purchasing agreement’s closing deadline, that Landis reasonably relied on those representations, and that Preview disregarded or failed to understand the obligations of a broker licensee under Wash. Rev. Code §18.86.030, the Court of Appeals erroneously reversed the entire judgment. Concluding that Landis remained successful in the unchallenged claim, the Court reversed the Court of Appeals in part and reinstated the awarded damages to Landis from this claim, and remanded to the trial court for further proceedings.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Futurewise v. Reed
facts: Petitioner Futurewise petitioned the Superior Court for King County to enjoin respondent Secretary of State Sam Reed from placing Initiative 960 on the November 2007 general election ballot, asserting that the initiative is unconstitutional insofar as its provisions making tax increases subject to referenda and requiring legislative supermajorities to increase taxes would effectively amend the Washington State Constitution without complying with the amendment process. The superior court granted summary judgment for Reed, ruling that the constitutionality of the initiative is not subject to pre-election review. Futurewise appealed this decision directly to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Is the constitutionality of Initiative 960 subject to pre-election review?
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander’s opinion for a unanimous Court affirmed the superior court, concluding that the only types of pre-election challenges to initiatives that are justiciable are challenges that assert that an initiative does not meet the procedural requirements for placement on the ballot and challenges that assert that the subject matter of an initiative is beyond the initiative power. Thus, as Initiative 960, whatever its practical effect may be, does not purport to amend the Washington State Constitution and its subject matter is within the legislative power, its constitutionality is not subject to pre-election review.

title: In re disciplinary proceeding against Holcomb
facts: The respondent Washington State Bar Association’s disciplinary board suspended petitioner James Holcomb from the practice of law for six months after it found that Holcomb violated Washington Rules of Professional Conduct 1.8(a), which restricts business transactions between attorneys and their clients, and 1.7(b), which prohibits conflicts of interest that materially limit an attorney’s representation of their client, when he sought and obtained interest free loans from a client. Holcomb appealed the disciplinary board’s decision to the Supreme Court of Washington, asserting that he did not violate any rules of professional conduct by engaging in a financial transaction with a client insofar as the source of funds for the loans was a revocable trust, that the sanction imposed is disproportionate in light of the fact that his actions were negligent rather than knowing, and that the disciplinary board erred in its consideration of mitigating and aggravating factors.
questions: Did Holcomb’s actions violate Washington Rules of Professional Conduct 1.8(a) and 1.7(b)? Is a six month suspension from the practice of law a disproportionate sanction? Did the disciplinary board err in its consideration of aggravating and mitigating factors?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for the Court affirmed Holcomb’s six month suspension, concluding that Holcomb’s actions violated Rule 1.8(a) insofar as the terms of the loan transactions were not fair and reasonable to his client and violated Rule 1.7(b) insofar as Holcomb’s representation of his client was materially limited by the conflict of interest (as Holcomb deliberately prolonged his representation of his client in order to continue taking out loans). The Court also held that a six month suspension from the practice of law is a proportionate sanction given that Holcomb acted knowingly and caused injury to his client. Finally, the Court found that the disciplinary board properly considered the absence of a prior disciplinary record and personal or emotional problems as mitigating factors and a dishonest or selfish motive, multiple offenses, and substantial experience in the practice of law as aggravating factors.

title: Ingram v. Department of Licensing
facts: Respondents Paul Ingram and Bryan Delong sought review in Kittias County Superior Court for the 90-day suspension of their driver’s licenses by petitioner Department of Licensing and the enforcement of the State’s Implied Consent law Wash. Rev. Code §46.20.308 for driving under the influence of an intoxicant. They challenged the suspensions on the ground that their respective license suspension hearing officers should not have admitted a blanket declaration regarding the breath testing machines submitted by the State toxicologist before the end of the hearing, because the declaration was not specifically admissible under any of the relevant statutes and regulations. The Superior Court reversed the suspensions by suppressing the results of both breath alcohol tests, and awarded Ingram and Delong monetary judgment. The Department of Licensing appealed to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the license suspension hearing officers have the proper authority to receive, admit, and weigh State documents as relevant evidence offered before the end of the hearing?
conclusions: Justice Tom Chambers’ opinion for the Court heldthat pursuant to the Department of Licensing rules in effect at the time of the respondents’ hearings, former Wash. Admin. Codes §§308-103-100, -120, -150(9), the hearing officers had full authority to rule on the admissibility of relevant evidence offered before the end of the hearing. Furthermore, once the hearing officer found the State toxicologist’s documents relevant as evidence, no further legal basis for admission was required. Finding the hearing officers committed no error of law; the Court reversed the Superior Court ruling, reinstated the 90-day suspensions, and vacated the monetary judgment.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: American Safety Casualty Insurance Company v. Olympia
facts: Respondent American Safety Casualty Insurance Company, surety for Katspan, Inc., filed suit against the petitioner city of Olympia in the Superior Court for Thurston County in an attempt to recover additional compensation for construction work that Katspan had performed for the city. The superior court granted summary judgment for the city of Olympia, ruling that American Safety Casualty Insurance Company had failed to comply with a provision in the contract between Katspan and the city of Olympia that requires that any cause of action under the contract be filed within 180 days of the close of the project. Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the city of Olympia had implicitly waived its right to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract when it agreed to negotiate a settlement with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company. American Safety Casualty Insurance Company appealed this decision to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: Did the city of Olympia implicitly waive its right to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract when it agreed to negotiate a settlement with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company?
conclusions: Justice Bridge’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals, concluding that the city of Olympia had not waived its right to to demand compliance with the provisions of the contract insofar as any waiver of such rights must be unequivocal and the city’s actions, in light of the fact that the city stated on several occasions in correspondence with American Safety Casualty Insurance Company that it reserved its right to demand strict compliance with the contract, were at best equivocal.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition

title: Christensen v. Ellsworth
facts: Petitioner Ed Christensen filed a complaint for unlawful detainer against respondent Richard Ellsworth after Ellsworth failed to make a rental payment and failed to respond to a notice to vacate the premises. The court entered an order of default and a writ of restitution when Ellsworth failed to appear. Christensen subsequently sought a default judgment based upon the order of default. Ellsworth responded by moving to vacate the order of default, asserting that the unlawful detainer action was prematurely commenced insofar as it failed to comply with Washington Revised Code §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action. In particular, Ellsworth maintained that although the unlawful detainer action was filed five days after Christensen posted the notice to vacate the premises, it was premature insofar as Washington Court Rule 6(a) excludes weekends and holidays in calculating time periods of less than seven days. The trial court granted summary judgment for Ellsworth, ruling that Christensen failed to provide sufficient notice as required by §59.12.030(3). Upon appeal, the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed.
questions: Does Washington Court Rule 6(a)’s time computation rule apply to §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst’s opinion for a unanimous Court reversed the Washington Court of Appeals and remanded the case, concluding that Washington Court Rule 6(a)’s time computation rule does not apply to §59.12.030(3)’s requirement that three days notice be provided period prior to filing an unlawful detainer action as this requirement is not one that deals with the mechanics of the operation of the superior court and the plain meaning of §59.12.030(3) indicates that its drafters intended for three days to mean three calendar days.
result: petitioning party received a favorable disposition
